utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. There were two matters I wanted to address before I got back to the substance of my remarks. One was regarding something I said yesterday about the Joint Command and our efforts to obtain documents relating to the Joint Command from -- from the Serbian authorities. There is an RFA in connection with that that is admitted into evidence; that's RFA 1317. And the response to that RFA indicated that the Joint Command was established by oral order of the FRY president in June 1998, and that it ceased to operate in October 1998. And the other matter was -- I don't know if you want to hear from me on this, Your Honour, but this has to do with a discussion we had yesterday on whether you can rely on a statement of an accused as evidence against a co-accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And this is in relation to Exhibit 949, the interview of General Pavkovic. As we discussed, this has been admitted into evidence pursuant to the Trial Chamber order of the 10th of October. We would submit, Your Honour, that it is relevant and probative evidence, as it goes to the existence of the Supreme Command and Mr. Milutinovic's participation in it. We rely on four points -- I see Mr. O'Sullivan is standing.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I don't mean to pre-empt any submissions, and I apologise to Mr. Hannis and the Chamber, but I would hope that Mr. Hannis refers to the submission that they made on the 18th of August, 2006, in support of tendering this -- this series of interviews that the OTP took. Their position is clearly spelled out in a submission of 18 August, 2006, and if he's changing that -- I say he cannot change the position he took in this filing, and I know I'm pre-empting his submission, but his submission has to be based on what the Prosecution filed when they moved for you to admit these statements from the bar table.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What was that submission?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I'm looking at the Prosecution's reply 18 August 2006, paragraph 44, the Prosecution said: "The statements given by the accused to the Prosecution are admissible pursuant to Rule 89(C) against the accused who made them. They are also admissible against co-accused, except those parts that go to the acts and conduct or the mental state of the co-accused." So they didn't offer them in relation to the acts and conduct or the mental state of the co-accused. That was their submission, and you admitted those statements on that basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. My point is that the existence of the Supreme Command and those who are members of it isn't an act of the accused or conduct of the accused. May I proceed with my other comments?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. The points we rely on, Your Honour, is: one, the Trial Chamber has broad discretion to admit and rely on evidence; number two, the common-law rules are modified at the Tribunal, especially with regard to hearsay; number three, the right to cross-examine a witness is not absolute; and number four, fairness to the Prosecution. With regard to the Trial Chamber's discretion, Rule 89(A) provides that you shall not be bound by the national rules of evidence. Rule 89(C) and (D) guide your decision in relying on Mr. Pavkovic's statement as evidence against any of the co-accused, and they say: "A Chamber may admit any relevant evidence which it deems to have probative value" subject to the safe-guard that "a Chamber may exclude evidence if its probative value is substantially outweighed by the need to ensure a fair trial." Not merely outweighed but substantially outweighed. So we say there's nothing in the Rules of Procedure and Evidence which prevents you from relying on General Pavkovic's statement as evidence against any of the other accused. Secondly, the common-law rules are modified at the Tribunal, especially regarding hearsay. In many jurisdictions, there -- there is a rule that allows for the admission of an accused's statement as evidence against a co-accused in certain circumstances. One of them is in my jurisdiction, it has to do with the co-conspirator exception to hearsay. In Canada, there's a case called Carter and the Carter rule. I realise both of those deal with statements of a co-conspirator in the context -- in the course of the conspiracy and in furtherance of the conspiracy, generally speaking. So it's not 100 per cent applicable to this situation where at the time Mr. Pavkovic gave his interview, our joint criminal enterprise is no longer functioning, except to the extent that - you may argue - that the members of the joint criminal enterprise may have a continuing interest in trying to hide evidence about the existence of the JCE and any criminal conduct they might have engaged in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I take it the exceptions you're referring to just now are things said in the course of the conduct of the enterprise and, therefore, are part of the res gestae of the crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour, and they are deemed to have more reliability because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That would be admissible in most jurisdictions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- that's a rather different situation from what we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I agree this is a different situation, because once the conspiracy or the joint criminal enterprise has ended, or once people have been arrested or charges filed, the playing field is changed, and the motivations of those individuals are much different, but you have to look at it in the context of whether or not -- one of the factors you should consider is whether or not the statement by the accused in question is inculpatory as to him or exculpatory as to him. For example, if I'm the one making a statement, and I'm talking about something that Mr. Stamp did and I'm putting him in trouble, I'm saying things that lead you to believe that he engaged in criminal conduct and I'm putting myself out of it; that's less reliable than something where I put myself in trouble just as much as Mr. Stamp. So that's a factor that you should look at. Now, the right to cross-examine a witness is not absolute. Our own rules, 92 bis and 92 quater, allow for the admission of evidence of unavailable witnesses, even if it goes to the acts and conduct of the accused. The fact that it may go to the acts and conduct of the accused is a factor that could be relied on in keeping out the evidence, but it's not automatically disqualified. And certainly we agree that an accused's statement raises particular concern that somebody with the motive to exculpate himself might try to shift the blame to others while being able to avoid cross-examination. We say that's addressed in two ways here at the Tribunal different from domestic jurisdictions. One is ICTY cases are heard by professional Judges and not lay jurors; secondly, Mr. Pavkovic's evidence can and should be considered in the totality of all of the evidence. I think Your Honour made the analogy yesterday about the skunk in the jury room. We respectfully submit that Your Honours are able to ignore the smell of the skunk. An additional safe-guard is that the accused may not be convicted solely on the basis of uncorroborated hearsay evidence. Other factors that go into the determination in this Tribunal about whether statements or prior testimony of unavailable witnesses, witnesses who can't be cross-examined for one reason or another, include the probative value of the evidence, its reliability, its relevance, and the circumstances under which it was given, was it under oath, was it signed and acknowledged. In this case we have a tape-recorded interview. Is it consistent with or corroborated by other evidence? Is it first-hand? How close was the witness to the actual events? And the accused -- the co-accused opportunity to introduce countervailing evidence. In this Tribunal in the Martic case, we had the situation where Milan Babic was an insider witness who testified at the trial but died before his cross-examination was completed. In that case, upon application of the Prosecution, the Trial Chamber and the Appeals Chamber agreed that it was appropriate to allow that evidence in, even though cross-examination had not been completed. The Trial Chamber stated that corroboration would be required of any evidence which had not been cross-examined upon, and the accused, Martic, was offered an opportunity to tender other evidence in rebuttal. In this case with the testimony -- or with the evidence and prior testimony of Dr. Rugova, you accepted our application to tender his evidence, even though it did go to the acts and conduct of some of the accused because you found it was relevant, probative and consistent with other evidence. In Aleksovski, a case before this Tribunal, the testimony and documents of Admiral Domazet given in the Blaskic trial were ruled admissible, noting that the weight or probative value will usually be less than given to a witness who has been cross-examined, and that certainly makes sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, let me leave you in no doubt about what my difficulty is with all this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You have chosen to put all the accused together. It's by your acts that you prevent on accused being able to call another as a witness and cross-examine him. And let me illustrate the situation with an example from our own case. You're going to rely on things said by a man called Perisic, and you have chosen not to call him as a witness for reasons which you must have and which are not immediately clear to me, but -- but they may be -- they may well be justified. But by relying on hearsay there, you're not inhibiting the Defence from calling him as a Defence witness and challenging his evidence in some way or trying to present him in a different way in different circumstances, but the accused here can't do that with Pavkovic, and that's where I find a fundamental difference from all the examples and all the circumstances you invite us to consider here. However, don't let me stop you illustrating the point further. I just want to be sure that you understand my -- my difficulty with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I do understand, I do understand your point, Your Honour, and I actually had come to the end of my examples. The last point I wanted to make was with regard to fairness to the Prosecution, that's a concept that we say extends to all the parties, including the Prosecution, and it's difficult to see. In Aleksovski, I think, the Appeals Court noted that it's difficult to see how a trial can be considered fair where the accused is favoured at the expense and the Prosecutor -- beyond a strict compliance with those fundamental protections. And I'm not saying that if you decide not to allow that, that you're being unfair to us; I just say that because that is one of the principles involved. Your Honour, that's my submission with regard to that, and as I say this particular evidence about the existence of the Supreme Command is -- is not at the same degree of inculpatory evidence as -- as maybe some other things that General Pavkovic could have said or may have said that we're not proposing to have you consider against other accused. And we say there is other evidence indicating the existence of that body at that time. That's all I had to say about that at that time. We -- we can make a written submission, if that's helpful to you, or if you feel you have enough, I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There is no need to make a written submission at this stage on any matter. We'll be content with the oral submissions of the party.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you for that opportunity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan, I'm reluctant to have regular interruptions of what Mr. Hannis has said.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Will you allow me to respond?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: On this point?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If you really think it's necessary. You --

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, I just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, if you are going to, it will be after the completion of Mr. Hannis's submission.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You can raise the matter then.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- Your Honour. Next, I wanted to talk about some of the crime base evidence. We didn't hear a lot of argument from most of the Defence counsel earlier this week contesting the crime base evidence. Mr. Ivetic raised some points, but for the most part I don't recall the others making much of an issue of that. We say there is more than ample evidence in this case at this stage for you to find that the crimes alleged did occur. And what I propose to do, Your Honour, unless you find it not helpful at all, was just quickly go through each of the scheduled deportation and killing incidents and name for you the witnesses who testified about each one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That will be extremely helpful, Mr. Hannis. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, the first is paragraph 72(a) and 72(a)(i) of the indictment which talks about the deportation from various villages in the Orahovac municipality. The witnesses who testified to Orahovac deportation include: Agim Jemini, Reshit Salihi and Ali Hoti. That was as to paragraph 72(a), which related to Celine. The witnesses who testified to paragraph 72(a)(i) and which was regarding the Krusha e Madhe, Bela Crkva, and Orahovac municipality generally include: Ali Hoti, Reshit Salihi, K25, Sabri Popaj and Isuf Zhuniqi or Zhuniqi. With regard to paragraph 75(b), that's murders in relation to Bela Crkva, the witnesses who testified about that were: Isuf Zhuniqi, Sabri Popaj, K25, and Agim Jemini. And paragraph 75(c), another killing incident, this is in regard to Mala Krusa, the witnesses who testified were: Mehmet Avdyli; Lutfi Ramadani; K25; John Sweeney, and he made some documentaries about that case, which are Exhibits P114 and 115; Ali Hoti also testified about some portion about that. I want to spend a little time to talk about this one, because Mr. Ivetic raised yesterday an issue about the perpetrators and suggested, I think, that this was a -- this was a local vendetta and didn't involve really any police. First of all, with regard to what forces surrounded the town before the killings occurred, you have the evidence from -- from K25 that on March 25th, he was told to go to Mala Krusa and his -- his unit set up a blockade. They were supposed to basically hold the line while mop-up operation was being conducted from the direction of Bela Crkva, Orahovac, and Velika Hoca. There were four PJP companies deployed for operations in the area south of Orahovac, and this witness explained on -- on a map, P109 and P2372, showing the various locations of VJ MUP, PJP, and military vehicles deployed at the time of this operation. He showed three tanks and four other VJ vehicles on the map in the area of Mala Krusa. Mr. Ramadani also talked about the tanks and anti-aircraft artillery weapons and armoured cars surrounding the village. On Exhibit IC72, he marked the main road, the road into the village, where the APCs and the tanks were stationed, and he marked the house where the -- the MUP gathered. He described the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, sorry, if I may interrupt -- sorry, I thought you were going through 72, but it's actually 75 you are going through?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. This -- this is the killings in Mala Krusa.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Yes, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: He described that the men with the vehicles wore black and multi-coloured camouflage uniforms. He says that the -- the army was in the mountains around the village and on the main road, while the policemen were the ones who were actually in the streets of the village. Mehmet Avdyli told you that he woke up to the sound of tanks on the 25th of March, and that they were firing in the upper part of the forest. Then he says that the forces started to burn down the village. He described MUP policemen wearing blue camouflage uniforms. He says they went to Dimitrije Nikolic's cafe in Mala Krusa on the 25th and 25th. As to the forces that actually did the killing, Lutfi Ramadani says that among the people in the village in different uniforms, he noticed also some local villagers, and he named several of the Nikolic family: Dimitrije Ranko, Momcilo, Sava, Zlatko, and -- and two or three other locals. He says they were all in uniform and armed, but with them there were other uniformed people who the villages did not know, and the locals were leading these others through the village, entering houses and setting them on fire. Inside the village, he only saw policemen. As he said -- as another witness said, the army was on the main road and in the mountains. There was a policeman in a black uniform, who with one of the locals separated the men from the women and children, then searched and ill-treated the men and took them to the Batusha barn where the women then were ordered to leave and the men were ordered to kneel down. There were many policemen along the road that the men walked on, on the way to the barn. Some they knew and some they didn't know. He didn't see the local policemen but only the others. After the witness fled from the barn, he saw policemen he did not know and also some of the locals near the barn. He recognised Stanko and Rade Nikolic, among others. Mehmet Avdyli saw men wearing green camouflage uniforms, and some wearing a combination of green camouflage and a plain green shirt, and people in the MUP blue camouflage uniform in the village. He describes a group of 15 policemen in dark blue and green camouflage, not all had the same uniform. And these were the ones who escorted them to the Batusha barn. He didn't know these policemen; they weren't locals. He did hear one of his neighbours address one of the shooters, saying Momcilo, is that you? He believed that was referring to Momcilo Nikolic, one of the local Serbs. Now, in connection with that, we have Exhibits 2357, which was a list that Lutfi Ramadani had prepared listing the local inhabitants who assisted or participated in the execution, that included several of the Nikolics, and Exhibits P2333 and 2335 were an RFA we had sent requesting information on the local Serbs from Mala Krusa as to any membership in the MUP or the VJ, and 2335 is the response, which indicated that several of them were members of -- or people with those names were members of the reserve police force in Prizren SUP. Exhibit P2850 is the personnel file for Zvezdan Nikolic, which confirms he was a fireman in the SUP of Prizren, and that, indeed, he was born in Mala Krusa and the son of Dimitrije Nikolic, who was identified by the witnesses as being present on that day. Now, the suggestion that this was a local vendetta goes counter to all the evidence and to a common-sense interpretation of what you've heard about who was out there and what they were doing. The mass murder of more than a hundred men occurred in the context of a big anti-terrorist operation that was going on throughout Orahovac and Prizren at the time. There was coordination of forces between the military and the MUP. The VJ was on the mountains and on the main road; and the MUP was going into the village. The VJ units were stationed so close to the PJP, they had direct oral communication with them. It's not reasonable, we say, in this context to assume that it would just happen that the whole village was being destroyed and a hundred men were being killed and the entire female population is being forced out. It's counter to our intelligence to believe that this was done by some rogue elements unnoticed by the VJ and the MUP that were stationed there for this operation. The witnesses testified that the expulsion of the women and the search and killing of the men was done in collaboration with local Serbs. It was not done entirely by local Serbs, it was done by policemen who were not from the village as well. K25 testified that the local Serb reservists were assigned duties of reserve policemen. Also of note, only the Albanian houses in Mala Krusa were completely burned and destroyed. The Serb and Roma houses were in perfect condition when Lutfi Ramadani returned in mid-June. The crime site, the barn, was dynamited and all the evidence destroyed, which we suggest is evidence of intent on the part of someone, probably the perpetrators, to hide what had happened. And up until this time, no investigation of this particular killing has occurred, even though there's been public information about some of the perpetrators. That was testified to by John Sweeney, and he indicated they actually managed to track down some of them in Serbia. Some documentary evidence relating to this incident, Your Honour, is found at Exhibit P2015, which is a Joint Command order of 23rd March 1999, to "provide assistance to the MUP in crushing and destroying Siptar terrorist forces in the Orahovac, Suva Reka, and Velika Krusa sector." And that document, we say, is important for you to look at in connection with this event, because it explicitly assigns tasks to particular units, the 549th Motorised Brigade, in the villages of Orahovac, which are indictment cites as listed below, and I'll detail it in a moment. It clearly states that the VJ units are to support MUP units, and it states that the Joint Command shall: "Command and control all forces during combat operations." The relevant details of that order include item 2, which assigns as a task to support MUP forces in the general area of Orahovac and Velika Krusa; item 4 mentions explicitly that the VJ should support the MUP forces in Bela Crkva and Velika Krusa, which equals the Krusha e Madhe village. The goal, according to the order, is to block, among others, Mala Krusa, Velika Krusa, Brestovac, and other villages. Item 5.1 calls for the 549th Motorised Brigade to blockade the line along the villages of Bela Crkva, in a joint action with VJ and MUP carry out -- carry all-out attack on the axis of villages around Bela Crkva, Velika Krusa. The more immediate task is to break-up and destroy the Siptar terrorist forces in the villages of Celine, Velika Krusa, and Mala Krusa. Related is Exhibit P1981, this is the brigade level order signed by Colonel Delic on destroying terrorist forces in the general sector of Retimlje and lifting a blockade of the Suva Reka-Orahovac road. This called upon at page 4, battle group 1 in cooperation with the 37th PJP Detachment and two platoons of MUP to energetically attack and destroy major individual targets using hardware to overpower and destroy the Siptar terrorist forces in Mala Krusa. Battle group 3 was to coordinate their actions with our forces in taking control of the villages of Mala Krusa and Celine, among others. Exhibit P1995 shows that the operation lasted from the 25th to the 29th of March in the relevant areas; that it involved in the neighbourhood of 2.000 men, 21 tanks. It also lists the MUP-PJP units that were deployed. It indicates that coordination among the forces and with the MUP forces were functioning well, and that it was under the Joint Command of the MUP and the VJ forces. K25 confirmed that the first paragraph of Exhibit P1995 describe accurately the operation he took part in, and that it lists his unit as participating in the operation. He confirms that MUP-PJP was partaking in the action. I'm not going to go through all of them, Your Honour. That was one in particular I wanted to go into some detail, but we say that you have heard evidence in this case, and you have evidence in the form of the documents, that will assist you in finding that there is reliable evidence upon which you can find that these crimes did indeed occur. With regard to paragraph 72(b), this is deportations from Prizren, you heard from three different -- or four different witnesses: Rexhep Krasniqi, Mr. Latifi, and Mr. Kreyziu - I can't pronounce his name - and I believe you also had evidence pursuant to 92 bis (C) or 92 ter, I'm not sure at what time we filed the motion regarding Mr. Morina's evidence. With regard to Serbica, that's both a deportation site and killing site. As to -- to that event, you heard evidence from -- on deportations, you heard evidence from Xhevahire Rrahmani. With regard to the killings in Izbica, you heard from Milazim Thaqi and Mustafa Draga and Liri Loshi. Others witnesses regarding deportations in that municipality included Hadije Fazilu and Abdullah Salihu. Next, paragraph 72(d) and 75(d), this is both deportations and killings in Suva Reka municipality. Regarding deportations, you heard from Mr. Zogaj and Ms. Fondaj. And regarding the killings, you've heard from Hyseni and Shyrete Berisha, as well as an insider witness who was K83. Regarding Pec deportation site in paragraph 72(e), the witnesses who testified included Ndrec Konaj and Edison Zatriqi. Dr. Riedlmayer testified about the destruction. Paragraph 72, Kosovo Mitrovica, the witnesses included Aferdita Hajrizi, Sadije Sadiku, Mahmut Halimi. Pristina deportation counts for the town itself and for villages in the area of Pristina in -- this was listed in paragraph 72(g) and 72(g)(i), the witnesses included: Nazlie Bala, Emin Kabashi, K62 and K63, K14, K31, Baton Haxhiu and Lakic Djorovic all spoke about that. Paragraph 72(h) and paragraph 75(g), this is Djakovica, both deportation and killings. Regarding the deportations, Fuat Haxhibeqiri testified. Regarding the killings at Milos Gilic Street, you heard from young Dren Caka, Hani Hoxha, Lulzim Vejsa and (redacted) Paragraph 72(h) and paragraph 75(h), again deportations and a killing site. This is in the Meja area. You heard from Lizane Malaj, Merita Deda and Martin Pnishi. You also heard evidence related to this from some insider witnesses as well. K73 gave evidence related to this, as well as did K90. And we also heard from -- and Nike Peraj about the operation in that area. Paragraph 72(i) was deportation only in the Gnjilane municipality. The witnesses who testified it included Qamil Shabani, K81, and Abdylhaqim Shaqiri. Paragraph 72(j), Urosevac, witnesses included Bajram Bucaliu, who worked at the train station and provided the log from the train station; Florim Krasniqi; and Bedri Hyseni. Paragraph 72(k) and 75(k), some deportations and killings both in the Kacanik municipality. You've heard evidence from Sejdi Lami, Muharrem Dashi, Fadil Vishi, Isa Raka, and Hazbi Loku. Decani, paragraph 72(l), deportations, you heard witnesses -- evidence from witnesses K20, K58, and Mehmet Mazrekaj. Paragraph 72(m) and 75(i) relates to Vucitrn municipality and deportations and a killing in connection with the convoy. You heard from Fedrije Xhafa, Shukri Gerxhaliu and Sabit Kadriu. And those are the crime base witnesses. Your Honours, I next want to address in connection with that, some issue regarding perpetrator identification. I'm certain you'll recall that early in the case, there was -- it was apparent that there was some confusion among the witnesses about perpetrators. Some used the term "soldiers" to identify what appears to be three different types of groups; some used the term "policemen"; some used the terms "paramilitaries." It seemed from the evidence that there's some overlap on how the crime base witnesses used those terms to describe the perpetrators. We think, now that you've heard all their evidence, there is some reason to understand why there is that confusion. There was also confusion about the colours. I don't know if the Court has had this, but we have made a request from CLSS to provide us some explanation about how there is some confusion based on how certain words for colours are used in Albanian Albania, in Albanian that's spoken in Albania, and Albanian that's spoken in Kosovo, and also you have some evidence about the different uniforms that the different forces wore. In General Lukic's interview, which is in evidence and it's -- I'm sorry, I don't have the exhibit number in front of me, but at page 54 of that transcript of the videotape which is ERN V000-3910, he tells us that PJP units had blue camouflage uniforms or green camouflage uniforms, that the SAJ and the JSO had green camouflage uniforms. So PJP had either or both. General Lukic went on to say that blue camouflage uniforms basically were worn for urban task, whereas green would be worn when carrying out tasks outside the urban areas. One point we would like to argue from the evidence with regard to identification of the perpetrators is, Your Honours, we say from all of the evidence, even though you may not be able to tell from an individual crime base victim's description of who came to his or her village on that day, whether it was a policeman, and if it was a policeman whether he was PJP or SAJ or JSO or whether he was in the VJ or the reserve or military territorial detachment or local civil defence of some sort, we say the evidence in this case indicates there were no large bands of armed men roving in Kosovo that weren't under the control of our accused. The number of VJ and MUP that were stationed in Kosovo at that time and their presence throughout Kosovo just excludes the reasonable possibility that any significant band of armed men roving around and doing mass killings or mass deportations could not be anybody except somebody in one of these -- one or more of these forces, we say, or under the control of, armed by, equipped by, and working with forces under the control of our accused. With that -- and I do now have that number for General Lukic's interview, that is Exhibit P948. Let me now move to some of the individual accused. General Ojdanic. I want to talk about his participation in the joint criminal enterprise. With regard to his authority, he was the highest-ranking military officer in the FRY at the time of our indictment. He was the Chief of the General Staff during peacetime, and when the state of war was declared, he became the Chief of Staff, the Chief of the Supreme Command Staff. Pursuant to the Law on Defence which is Exhibit P985 and the Law on the Army or the Law on the Armed Forces, P984, in that position he exercised de jure and, we say, de facto command over the VJ and units subordinated to it. After the declaration of a state of war on the 24th of March, we say he also exercised control over MUP units engaged in combat operations and other organs subordinated to the VJ or acting in concert with the VJ. This is under the -- under the FRY law on the -- on defence, which is our Exhibit P985. On the 19th of April, 1999, we have an order from General Ojdanic, this is Exhibit P1460, as Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command and citing as authority Article 17 of the Law on Defence and the order of the president of the FRY. He's subordinating MUP units to the VJ. How did he contribute to the JCE? We say he did so through several channels. He used the VJ General Staff to plan, direct, and coordinate the operations and activities of the forces of the FRY, in Kosovo, that furthered the JCE's purpose of altering the ethnic balance by removing hundreds of thousands of Kosovo Albanians. General Ojdanic assisted in the planning and coordination of the deployment of troops to Kosovo that committed the crimes charged in the indictment. In the minutes of the collegium of the General Staff for the 25th of February, 1999, this is Exhibit P941, at page 12 there is a reference made to the resubordination of units from outside of Kosovo to VJ units operating in Kosovo. And on the 21st of January, 1999, General Ojdanic presided over a meeting of the collegium, and this is P939, particularly at pages 24 through 26, in which a plan of operation against the KLA during spring-time was discussed in detail. Now, on the face of it, it was a spring offensive that was a legitimate anti-terrorist operation, but we say in its implementation it included massive crimes that were committed in furtherance of the JCE. As the Chief of General Staff, he exercised his authority in other ways by ordering an increase in the troops' strength of the 3rd Army units. This was to be found in Exhibit P1487, suggestions to the 3rd Army command from the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command. And that's a document we've talked about before, too, that makes a reference to a Joint Command order. He did it also by mobilising reserve units. He further contributed by arming civilians. General Ojdanic was aware. He was aware of and involved in the arming of predominantly non-Albanian civilians into local or village defence units during a collegium meeting on -- I believe it's the 21st of January -- I'm sorry, it may be the 30th of December, 1998. It's P928. During that meeting it was suggested to General Ojdanic that some 60.000 Serb civilians could be mobilised outside the control of official organs. In another meeting of the collegium, Ojdanic was updated on the arming of civilians, the weapons that were being issued to them, and the manner in which these armed civilians would be incorporated into VJ operations. This is a meeting from 2 February 1999 and found in Exhibit P931 and the reference goes to page 23 of that meeting. We say this is important because you will see in the Joint Command orders, during the first week of the war, that there is particular reference to implementing and using the armed non-Siptar population in carrying out those operations. You will see that specific tasks are assigned for the non-Siptar population, in many cases to blockade an area or control a road. We say also that General Ojdanic's authority as head of the Supreme Command Staff was augmented by the fact that he was a member of the Supreme Defence Council and he directly participated in the formulation of policy and issued orders and instructions to his subordinates in further of the JCE. You have an order from the Supreme Command Staff dated the 12th of April 1999 in which Ojdanic subordinates forces of the MUP and civilian defence to the command of the 3rd Army. That's Exhibit P1483. As a member of the Supreme Command Staff he participated in strategy formulation, strategic-level decisions, and he commanded operations during the state of war that was declared on 24 March. The Supreme Command was headed by President Milosevic as the Supreme Commander, and it's clear that Ojdanic worked in collaboration with Milosevic on issues such as troop deployment and operations in Kosovo. We point to Exhibit P1495 from the 24th of May, 1999. VJ and MUP coordination is another aspect of Ojdanic's participation in the JCE. He encouraged it, he was involved in it, he issued orders, as we said before. He issued orders to formally subordinate MUP units engaged in combat operations. He also issued an order on the 29th of May, 1999, to the 3rd Army command, which is Exhibit P1920, urging the 3rd Army and subordinate units to now prepare for NATO's possible land invasion, and that order clearly shows that the MUP was resubordinated to the VJ. And that order, Your Honour, we say you should look at as well because he notes that up to this point in time, 29th of May, 1999, that the Pristina Corps has not been able to prepare for a possible NATO land invasion because they've been too busy being engaged in their anti-terrorist operations, evidence which we say shows General Ojdanic's awareness of what the VJ was doing in the first months of the war. We say that because of that order, because of the law, the MUP units engaged in combat operations were under the effective control of the VJ. We say that General Ojdanic had knowledge of the crimes that were being committed in furtherance of the JCE, and he was informed of these through various means, including international observers and as a function of his position in command organs. Regarding international observers, before the war was declared in March 1999, he had interactions with international observers, who told him that the VJ was acting improperly and illegally, using excessive force. The security -- UN Security resolutions were public knowledge. General Crosland spoke about presenting evidence regarding the evidence -- regarding excessive force being used in Kosovo and to which Ojdanic responded: "Force would be met with force." Now, I don't think it's clear from the evidence whether General Ojdanic viewed that tape, but it was presented to his staff, according to Colonel Crosland. And we say in this regard and in all other regards concerning General Ojdanic, we agree with Mr. Sepenuk. Read the collegium minutes. They're lengthy, they're extensive, a lot of it is, for me and maybe for Your Honours, boring and not so pertinent, but it's sort of impossible to pick and choose a sentence or a paragraph. You have to read the whole thing to get an understanding and flavour for the persons involved, their interactions. But we say what it shows is extremely detailed knowledge on the part of General Ojdanic and the General Staff or the Supreme Command Staff about what's happening on the ground. I mean, sometimes they talk about very minor individual events. One soldier has had frostbite and had toes amputated and there's a discussion about what they need to do about that because of some claim he might make for assistance after his army service is over. But they also talk about things that are going on at the international level, how Serbia's being viewed, how they're under pressure, how they're under scrutiny from the outside world and how that affects what they do and how they do it in Kosovo. So please do read those collegium minutes that are in evidence. Ojdanic's knowledge of events also derived from being in the position he held and as a result of the reporting structures within those organs. To reflect what I said, that they were extremely well-informed. Daily reports were sent up the chain of command, and you will see from the documents and you will know from the testimony you've heard that the reporting system within the VJ was well organised. Exhibit P2603 is a entitled "the methodology of work of Pristina Corps" signed by General Lazarevic on the 6th of January, 1999. It's a directive from the Pristina Corps command with detailed guidance on reporting obligations. And you'll see that those were complied with. That reporting went from the subordinate units of the Pristina Corps all the way to the top of the chain of command, to the Supreme Commander, Milosevic, on operational matters. And as an example of that, we point you to Exhibit P1480, which is described as a preparatory order from the Supreme Command. It's from General Ojdanic, as chief of the Supreme Command Staff, directed to General Pavkovic, as commander of the 3rd Army, to submit a proposal for a decision which then could be submitted at the Supreme Command Staff in the presence of the Supreme Commander. Also, in terms of being informed on what was happening on the ground, we point you to Exhibit P929, and this is a VJ collegium meeting at pages 33 and 34. This April 9th meeting you will see reference being made to some 400.000 refugees. So at the Supreme Command Staff they are aware in early April of what is happening with regard to the actions their units are taking in Kosovo and how thousands -- hundreds of thousands of refugees have come into being as a result. We say that General Ojdanic was also aware of crimes committed by certain volunteers in Kosovo. Exhibit P490 and P1943 refer to an order of the 20th of April, 1999, in which -- this is from the Supreme Command Staff. General Ojdanic refers to a report of the 3rd Army which sets out in detail the actual knowledge of the Supreme Command on the use of unscreened volunteers and the serious crimes committed by them in Kosovo. On the 13th of May, you heard evidence -- well, you didn't hear it on the 13th of May, but you heard evidence that on the 13th of May, 1999, General Farkas informed Ojdanic about this issue. That's when Ojdanic informed Milosevic the following day. This is from General Vasiljevic's testimony and from his statement, Exhibit P2594, paragraphs 59 to 62. Vasiljevic also briefed Ojdanic about these crimes, and we've heard evidence about the meeting that took place on the 17th of May chaired by Slobodan Milosevic, attended by Mr. Sainovic, General Pavkovic, General Ojdanic, Rade Markovic from the DB, and General Vasiljevic. Crimes against civilians, including murder and rape, problems with volunteer groups, some of these are associated with the MUP, including the Skorpions and the Arkan's Tigers were discussed. It was at this meeting that Rade Markovic said that volunteers were "a necessary evil" that accompanied every war. However, it's not only at this meeting where allegations were made the crimes were being committed either by the police or by the VJ. You have Exhibit P1996 which are the MUP staff minutes of a meeting on the 7th of May 1999 where complaints are being made about crimes being committed primarily by the VJ, by army units. Now, more specifically we say that Ojdanic was informed of criminal acts against Albanian civilians by the MUP which was operating with the VJ. We have General Pavkovic's report dated 25 May 1999 on the noncompliance of MUP organs. That's Exhibit P1459. We say that's worthy of some attention by Your Honours. At paragraph 3, it says that MUP members were condoning criminal activities such as plunder by fellow MUP members, and it describes some of them are committing serious offences such as murder, rape, robbery against the Siptar civilian population in settlements or refugee shelters. And it complains that in spite of the April -- I believe April 18th order for subordination of MUP units, they had not subordinated themselves to the VJ. This is an issue in this case, and this is something that you will need to pay attention. But there's some interesting aspects to it, we say. This complaint from General Pavkovic comes on the 25th of May, 1999. Your Honour, that's three days after the indictment in case number IT-99 -- 99-37 was issued. That's an indictment that was signed by Louise Arbour, when she was the Prosecutor, and it's for the Kosovo case. It charges Milosevic, Ojdanic, and Minister Stojiljkovic, Mr. Sainovic. So three days before that indictment had been issued, and I believe it on the 22nd of April is the date that it was signed, it's file-stamped in the registry, I think, on the 23rd and became, I believe, public on the 24th of May. So on the 25th of May, General Pavkovic is writing this order saying: MUP hasn't been subordinate -- has not been subordinated to us in the army, they haven't done what they're supposed to do, and they've been committing a bunch of crimes. But this is almost five weeks after the original order. We haven't seen evidence in this case about ongoing complaints about MUP not subordinating itself to the army. We've had lots of joint combat operations that have been carried out under orders of the Joint Command where they're working together, and we've had post-action reports in evidence indicating that cooperation went well, they worked well together with the MUP. So we suggest you should view this evidence in the context of the time when it occurred and when the motivation might be. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did that indictment also include Mr. Milutinovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I believe it did. Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry I omitted him. And as I said, it notes that the army was well aware that the MUP -- that some MUP members and smaller units that "operate independently on the ground" were committing these serious offences against the civilian population. But there's no indication that any other action was taken by General Pavkovic or General Ojdanic. Now, I suppose the argument will be: Well, they -- they didn't subordinate themselves, so we can't do anything about it. But even if -- even if that were the case, we suggest that in the context of this conflict that's going on, the VJ has the substantial forces in this area. These are crimes occurring in their area of responsibility. At the least, there should be some reporting or information to civilian authorities or to MUP authorities and superiors about these crimes. We don't see any evidence of that. So despite knowledge of these crimes, we say General Ojdanic failed to take substantive measures to prevent commission of further crimes or to punish anyone for the ones that he knew about. We say this created an atmosphere of impunity which encouraged and instigate further crimes. And when you take that together with all the other evidence, we say it shows that General Ojdanic intended for those crimes to occur. The -- the reasonable inference that you can take from this is that the crimes charged were part of a common plan to alter the demographic balance in Kosovo, and thus part of the joint criminal enterprise that we've alleged. Ojdanic made contributions to that enterprise with the intent that he shared with the other members. Now, our fall-back position with regard to all the accused is that if you don't find responsibility under JCE, that you may find responsibility under 7(1) with regard to General Ojdanic on the basis of planning and ordering; or, in the alternative, that he aided and abetted the commission of such crimes. In that regard, we say he permitted and facilitated the involvement of VJ personnel and resources in combat activities in Kosovo. He knew that without the involvement of those units, the objectives of the JCE couldn't be achieved. And by implementing instructions from Milosevic as a member of the staff of the Supreme Command, as the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command, he lent material and moral support to the members of the JCE. And by abstaining from taking any substantive disciplinary measures, he encouraged and morally supported the direct perpetrators of those crimes against the Kosovo-Albanian population. We say he shared an intention to participate in the JCE with its other members. He knew the plan was being implemented, and he didn't exercise his authority to prevent or restrain it. And in connection with that, we point again to that order with suggestions for the 3rd Army, which is the one that makes reference to a Joint Command order that is -- that the Supreme Command Staff and General Ojdanic are aware of. Again, this is Exhibit P1487. The Joint Command is not a body provided for in the constitution or the Law on Defence or the Law on the Army. There doesn't seem to be any legal basis for it, yet General Ojdanic seems to be content and satisfied to go along with it. He doesn't order the 3rd Army to disregard it; he makes the suggestion that they might want to do some aspect of it differently. We say this shows his intention, his shared intention with the other members of the JCE. Likewise, we say evidence about the removal of certain high-level personnel show his intention -- his shared intention to participate in the JCE. Unlike his predecessor General Perisic, we say the evidence shows Ojdanic supported the involvement of VJ in combat activities in Kosovo under -- under conditions which General Perisic felt were in contravention of the VJ's legal mandate. This is evidence we've talked about a lot. General Perisic's letter of -- of 23rd of July, 1998, Exhibit P717, where he said, If the army is going to be used this way, Mr. Milosevic, you really need to declare a state of emergency. When General Ojdanic replaced General Perisic in late November, after that date you heard General DZ say there was a change in the attitude, there was a perceived change in the attitude and the way in which the army was used. We say this change occurred in part because Ojdanic was viewed as someone who was more willing to go along with what Milosevic wanted to do in Kosovo with the army. As Chief of the General Staff, we say he used his authority to facilitate the furtherance of the JCE. Now, while the removal of senior VJ officials like General Perisic was done on a basis of a decision by the FRY president, Mr. Milosevic, as Chief of the General Staff, Ojdanic makes recommendations to the Supreme Defence Council on personnel issues. You see that is referred to in the order on agreed facts of 11 July 2006. Now, in addition, pursuant to a decree by Milosevic, Ojdanic assisted in the replacement of officers who were opposed to the use of the VJ in Kosovo and the replacement of officers. We point you to Exhibits P799 through P803, a series of five documents. We say you can also see his intention, his shared intention with the other members of the JCE is shown by his actions in connection with breach of the October 1998 agreements. The build-up of troops and creation of training areas, we say, are examples of breaches of those agreements which were within Ojdanic's area of responsibility. In addition, you've heard from General Loncar of another example when he testified that Ojdanic refused to permit General DZ to inspect military brigades and weapons located in Kosovo, in spite of Ojdanic's acknowledgement that such monitoring was a part of the October agreements. That can be found at transcript page 7672. Ojdanic's superior responsibility, Mr. Stamp will be talking some -- about 7(3) responsibility, but I'll mention something here. Ojdanic had the material ability and obligation to enforce military discipline and to effect prosecution and punishment. The military justice system was properly functioning during the time-period of the indictment. You can see that in Exhibit 1917, the Supreme Command Staff report of 7 May 1999. We say after the declaration of war and pursuant to the order of the president and the Supreme Command Staff's order, that Ojdanic had command over MUP units that were subordinated to the VJ for combat operations. He had sufficient information available to put him on notice that units under his command were about to or had committed crimes, and he failed to take effective measures. Instead of putting his authority to use to end those widespread attacks against the civilian population, the few criminal cases that were prosecuted didn't really cover those serious crimes; rather, you'll see they're more focussed on crimes against the army: desertion, absence without authorisation, and other crimes related to infractions of VJ discipline. An exception, I guess I would add, is -- is theft. There were lots of prosecutions for theft and looting, but not for murder, not for war crimes. And you'll see this in reports on -- of the 3rd Army command organ on legal affairs on the work of military prosecutors and courts, Exhibits P1912, 1939, 1940, and 1941. For example, of the 91 proceedings mentioned in the Pristina Corps report about the status of military proceedings involving its members since 24 March 1999, none of them covered serious violations of law, of war, or international humanitarian law. That is Exhibit number P1182, dated the 15th of May. We say this systematic failure to investigate and properly prosecute resulted in extremely few war criminal cases ever being tried. According to the testimony of Lakic Djorovic, he was repeatedly faced by attempts to obstruct his investigations in criminal proceedings. We say Ojdanic's lack of effective and timely response demonstrates an intent to permit the occurrence of these crimes or, at the very least, the knowledge and lack of action in fulfilling the requirements of Rule 7(3). You'll recall General Vasiljevic's account of how this information first came to light for General Ojdanic, as far as General Vasiljevic knows. That's when General Farkas advised him. Ojdanic called Milosevic, an appropriate action. A meeting was scheduled, and he, General Ojdanic, ordered General Pavkovic to come up and brief him on what had been happening. They had a pre-meeting meeting before the big meeting on the 17th of May with Milosevic, Sainovic, and Rade Markovic. It seems clear, based on what General Vasiljevic tells us in his statement and evidence, that prior to coming up to brief General Ojdanic, General Pavkovic must have known about some of those crimes, because he explains how there were 800 bodies on the ground, and that he's been having discussions with the MUP and General Lukic about who's responsible for which of those 800 bodies, and how they'd sorted it out that the army was responsible for 270-some, and the MUP was saying that maybe 300 were theirs and the others were unaccounted for. So it seems that Pavkovic knew about these crimes but apparently had not reported it to General Ojdanic before that. But if that's the case, then it seems that General Ojdanic should have taken some action, some punishment, some discipline against General Pavkovic, and there's no evidence of any of that occurring. We say that shows an intention, a shared intent, by Ojdanic with the others that the crimes be committed. Now, I want to just address some of the remarks that Mr. Sepenuk made in regard to this. The basics of Mr. Sepenuk's argument seems to be that General Ojdanic was running a tight ship and reacting appropriately. He was removed from the Kosovo units by a few levels and dependent on the accuracy of the reports from the field. And he also says that the operations in the spring were a reasonable response to KLA and the NATO threat, and there wasn't any intention. But the VJ conduct in the field, we say, it was not in March 1999 directed at the NATO threat. Those forces, you'll see from the -- the 16 February order, I think it's 20 -- P2808, this is the 40-page directive or planning order from General Lazarevic. It has the subject number 455-1, the first in the series of those orders from which we find the 13 Joint Command orders in late March. The deployment of units were not at the borders, where you might expect if they were anticipating a NATO attack from Macedonia or Albania, but they were throughout Kosovo in the heartland, in the area where the KLA forces were but where our crimes occurred, the ones that are listed in the indictment. And these are consistent with the Joint Command orders and the combat reporting from the Pristina Corps and the subordinate unites. This involved many VJ and MUP units on an offensive over large sections of Kosovo and occurred on the dates of the crimes alleged in our indictment. It also involved the armed Serb civilians, the armed non-Siptar population which Ojdanic was aware of since at least February, based on what we see in the collegium minutes. And the way they conducted operations, excessive tactics. An example is from the commander of the 37th Brigade, where he made the comparison to using an elephant to kill a fly, I believe. All this meant that civilians would flee, as they did in 1998, even when there was no bombing. With regard to those armed civilians, Exhibit P931, which is a VJ collegium meeting, Ojdanic heard that there were 47.000 armed Serbs, that their wartime tasks were to defend villages and participate together with army units in any operations in the immediate vicinity. Ojdanic made no further comment upon hearing that. And as we've said, the Joint Command orders refer to using the armed non-Siptar population. So we have a VJ link to those armed civilians, who we say were armed by the VJ. And prior to this meeting, in P939, the 21 January 1999 collegium meeting, General Dimitrijevic had previously expressed a concern about Serbs in Kosovo radicalising. So he had an express concern about the attitude of the Serb civilians in Kosovo; and in a meeting after that, when General Ojdanic hears 47.000 of them are being armed, we say this is something that should put him on notice that crimes might occur. With regard to the Joint Command in the VJ collegium meeting of 21 January 1999, P939, Ojdanic makes reference to the Joint Command. So it's clear that even at that early date, he was aware of its existence. There was a comment about reporting problems and honouring October agreements. Ojdanic is presented with allegations that reporting some subordinate units to the General Staff isn't accurate. I think it's General Dimitrijevic that's talking about this, that some operations are presented as exercises and others described as responses to KLA provocation when that wasn't the case. Ojdanic doesn't seem to show in the meeting a proportional degree of concern about that. We point you to Exhibit P928 at page 10; P931 at pages 15 to 16; P938 at page 21; P933 at page 13. Reports don't show that it's the VJ initiating some attacks rather than the KLA. Instead, they claim the opposite. It is Dimitrijevic and General Andjelkovic who both mention this. Planning for the spring. The collegium minutes P929 and P939 corroborate the Joint Command orders in documents such as P995, the 549th Brigade post-operation analysis, describing combat operations in Kosovo where the indictment incidents occurred. And finally I want to say in connection with General Ojdanic, we say that he is criminally liable for his participation in the JCE. At the very least, he's incurred individual criminal responsibility under Article 7(1) in relation to ordering, planning, or aiding and abetting, and that he's also liable under Article 7(3). Next, I want to move to General Pavkovic. General Pavkovic had direct involvement in the joint criminal enterprise by planning, ordering, and implementing the use of the VJ in Kosovo to further the JCE's objective of basically ethnic cleansing, to alter the ethnic balance, to maintain Serb control in the province. He, too, was an integral part of the JCE through his active participation in the Joint Command, by providing tactical guidance and military support of the 3rd Army and its subordinate units. With regard to his command position, in 1998 he'd been commander of the Pristina Corps. In early 1999, we know that he was elevated to become commander of the 3rd Army. In both those positions, we say he had the authority to issue orders and require reporting from subordinates, and therefore had effective control over those units. The evidence shows that throughout 1998, General Pavkovic violated the Law on Defence by using the Pristina Corps in engagements within Kosovo without a declared state of war or emergency. Superior officers were aware of this, as was noted in General Perisic's letter, Exhibit P717. Mr. Pavkovic had effective control of the Pristina Corps in 1998, and was aware that crimes were being committed in Kosovo in terms of excessive force and the force against the civilian population, and he exhibited, we say, a willingness to disregard the rule of law. In 1999, after his elevation to command the 3rd Army, he had de jure and de facto control over the 3rd Army. In Exhibits P1946 and 1947, you see him requesting the resubordination of units outside of the 3rd Army to support 3rd Army combat operations. And as commander of the 3rd Army, Pavkovic had knowledge of the crimes being committed by his subordinate units. We say this was derived from his substantial presence on the ground in Kosovo. In his suspect interview, P949, at page 812, he indicated that 95 per cent of his time in Kosovo was spent at the forward command post. In addition, he had regular reports from his subordinates from the Pristina Corps. He had further information from the Joint Command, and we say he intended to participate in the joint criminal enterprise through his active role in the Joint Command. Colonel Pesic told us that he knew that General Pavkovic had attended Joint Command meetings in 1998, and from the minutes of the Joint Command in July through October of 1998, Exhibit 1468, you will see his regular attendance and participation in those meetings. Mr. Cvetic also testified that Pavkovic was a member of the Joint Command. From within this body, the Joint Command, operational plans were organised and later implemented, particularly by units under the command of General Pavkovic. A review of Joint Command orders shows that specific attention was paid to the use of the 3rd Army, the Pristina Corps, and its subordinate units. And in connection with General Pavkovic's role and participation with the Joint Command, we ask you to pay particular attention to Exhibit P2166. These are the minutes of a late October 1998 meeting of the interdepartmental staff for combatting terrorism in Kosovo-Metohija. I think the minutes are actually dated the 2nd of November, 1998, and Pavkovic is the one who is assigned the task of reporting on what the Joint Command has been doing for the previous several months. It goes into great detail about what they've done. This is a meeting, too, where it's discussed about whether the Joint Command should continue to exist, and the consensus is indeed that it should, with perhaps some change in membership. And you'll see the report on how many KLA they report to have killed in the process of those months and what strides they have made in their efforts. Pavkovic was the means to bring the overall command of the 3rd Army to fulfil the objectives of the JCE, and we say through his membership on the Joint Command, he intended the use of those units, including many that he knew to have committed crimes in 1998. Evidence that shows his intent. We say he intended for crimes to be committed in Kosovo in part by inciting his troops. Exhibit -- pardon me. The testimony of K73 included his reference to a gathering of members of that unit where General Pavkovic spoke to them. This is shortly before the declaration of the state of war, and he indicated to him that that was likely to happen and that: "Once NATO bombs begin to fall, we will rid our backs of Albanians." We say in light of all the evidence about what happened since that date, that that was an indication of the intent to carry out and implement the purposes of the joint criminal enterprise; that is, to solve the problem, the Kosovo problem, that had been going on for years by getting those Albanians out. We say that was not referring just to the KLA, but that was to all of them or as many of them as possible to bring it down to a manageable number where the Serbs could easily maintain effective control. It was just too hard. It was just too hard. They'd been trying for a long time to deal with the KLA, and the KLA is an insurgent army that sometimes would run and gun, attack from ambush, then go back to the village, take off their uniform, and mix in with the civilian population, a civilian population which by and large supported them, some with more enthusiasm than others, but at least they provided shelter and food, lodging. It was just too hard to try and sort it out anymore. And we say the evidence shows, and it's a logical inference, that this was the point where they had decided they weren't going to try and sort them out anymore; let's just kick them out and keep them out, and then we don't have to mess with it. It's too difficult, it's too hard, we've lost too many good men already. We say that's a reasonable inference you can draw from the evidence. The VJ was a professional army with a fully functioning reporting system. Those reports detail the status of operations and who was involved. Combat reports from the 549th, Colonel Delic's motorised brigade, indicate that joint operations with the MUP were successful. You see that in Exhibit P1995 from the 30th of March, 1999, right after many of the most serious crimes had occurred. Pavkovic was informed by General Lazarevic of the increased movement of population in Kosovo around the 30th of March, 1999. You hear that in Pavkovic's suspect interview, Exhibit P949 at page 8. Moreover, Pavkovic provided his superiors with detailed accounts of the situation in Kosovo. It's clear that he was substantially well informed. And I want to refer you now, one more time, to his suspect interview, P949, at page 18, a couple items I want to point to. In there, Pavkovic states that there was a conflict between Kosovo Albanian and non-Albanians, Serbs and Montenegrins, which was known from the previous historical situations and crimes always occurred when there were such conflicts. He also said that he didn't know who was taking identity cards from Albanians as they left the borders, especially through the border with Macedonia. It happened at Djeneral Jankovic or Kacanik, but he doesn't know who did it or who gave the order. He heard it was the 10th day of the campaign and the roads between Urosevac and Djeneral Jankovic were completely congested. So Pavkovic informed the Supreme Command Staff. He said that it must have been the MUP because although VJ controlled the border areas, the MUP controlled the border crossings. And at page -- I'm sorry, that's -- that's the end of that. After the NATO bombings began, Pavkovic, we say, after the order from the president and General Ojdanic, as Chief of the Command Staff to resubordinate the MUP to the VJ -- we say after that date he had de jure authority over the MUP and its subordinate units engaged in combat operations. And we've talked about the 17 May meeting where the discussion was held regarding crimes in Kosovo with Mr. Milosevic and Mr. Sainovic. In connection with that we say Pavkovic is additionally responsible for the concealment of crimes and we talk about the murders that occurred in Izbica. You heard from Dr. Tomasevic that General Pavkovic told her that her assistance would be needed in connection with some "asanacija," the cleansing or sanitation of the territory. You heard her testimony about the bodies that she examined, and from the other evidence we know that these were the bodies that were dug-up from Izbica. From the other evidence we've suggested to you before that the digging up of bodies and the then taking them to Serbia suggests some guilty knowledge on the parts of those engaged. Mr. Thaqi told you that he witnessed the mass murder of those men who were buried there and who were among those who were exhumed from Izbica. Shared intent. We say General Pavkovic shared the intent of other members of the JCE through his active participation in the Joint Command in planning, ordering, and providing material support to further JCE objectives through his position of authority over the 3rd Army and subordinates. He openly shared information regarding the current state of the 3rd Army with persons outside his chain of command. We have evidence from General Loncar that Pavkovic gave information directly to Sainovic, further that Pavkovic often met with President Milosevic without informing his superiors. We have evidence of that from General Vasiljevic in his statement Exhibit P2589 and in the transcript at T15978. General Loncar's evidence about this is in his witness statement at P2521. Failure to prevent and punish. We say Pavkovic had knowledge that crimes were being committed that made him aware of a real or reasonably foreseeable risk that other crimes would be committed, and that he failed to take reasonable measures to punish or prevent. Reports that he had served to put him at least on inquiry notice. We say he disregarded the seriousness of those offences, and this is demonstrated in part through the nominal prosecution of persons for crimes against civilians. See Exhibit P955, a summary of review of prosecutions; Exhibit P831, report of activities undertake by the MUP to uncover war crimes; and P939, report on the work of the military prosecutor. We say Pavkovic should have implemented investigations into allegations and he failed to take those reasonable steps. In the alternative we say he, too, through his willingness to provide material support with the knowledge that crimes were being committed substantially contributed to fulfilling the JCE's objectives, and he knew that without that support of the VJ, JCE wouldn't succeed in meeting those objectives. We say that Pavkovic willingly allowed and intended for the VJ to be used in Kosovo and in coordination with the MUP to carried out those crimes in furtherance of the JCE. He was aware of the widespread nature of crimes being committed within Kosovo. See Exhibit P2508, statement of General DZ, who had reported the mass depopulation of villages throughout Kosovo. Further, his failure to take reasonable steps to punish and prevent only encouraged and morally supported the perpetration of further atrocities. Based on the foregoing, we say the evidence shows at this stage, it meets the burden that General Pavkovic aided and abetted the commission of the crimes charged, and he substantially contributed to the commission of those crimes through his support. Your Honours, this would be a good time for me to break, if that's convenient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ideal, Mr. Hannis. We'll resume at 11.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I just wanted to respond to some of the remarks that Mr. Ackerman made regarding General Pavkovic before I move on to talk about General Lazarevic. Mr. Ackerman told us that war is hell, and the gist of some of his remarks seemed to be just basically: Well, these things happen. Stuff happens in war, and suggests that no commander could control these kinds of things. I understand the essence of his remarks, but a professional army has a system to eliminate as much as possible the rogue actions of soldiers. They have training, they have leadership, and this isn't like kids in a city street in a gang in New York or Detroit or Los Angeles. Some young men with guns in combat will commit crimes, but when that happens there's an obligation for commanders to take a proportionate response and that means more than just charging a few individual perpetrators. And this war was different than some other modern wars in that it wasn't a high-intensity, high-paced conventional war with one conventional army against another on the ground. NATO was bombing but didn't have ground troops. The confrontation was between the Serb VJ, a modern professional army, with the KLA. It was a much superior force using heavy weapons against a relatively smaller and more poorly trained and equipped force with a substantial civilian population in the middle. Mr. Ackerman suggested that we were bringing Mr. Pavkovic here as based on guilt by association. That's not quite correct. Pavkovic was a commander, and the units in Kosovo were his subordinate units. Crime base witnesses and documents put his subordinates in the areas of crimes at the time those crimes occurred. He was not far removed; he was in Kosovo. And he tells us in his suspect interview that he was at the forward command post 95 percent of the time when he was there. He was aware of crimes during the war, for example, Izbica, and the mass movement of civilians coincident with his force's operations. I believe Mr. Ackerman referred to international witnesses talking about 1998, but they don't just talk about 1998, they talk about activities in 1999 as well. He addressed the issue of General Perisic and his complaints about General Pavkovic. He suggests that if it was really such a problem, Perisic could have just removed him. We suggest the law -- the laws that are in evidence don't support that. It does not appear that under the law that Perisic could remove a general; he didn't have that authority. It's in the SDC rules and laws. It's the FRY president acting on the recommendations of the Chief of Staff who can decide whether to accept a recommendation and remove a general officer. Perisic could do that with a lower-level officer and with a colonel and below, I believe, is what the laws say. Mr. Ackerman suggested that the Prosecution's evidence about Pavkovic going outside the chain of command was -- was a red herring. We say it's not, Your Honour. It's relevant to at least a couple of things, and you'll see that there is discussion about that in some of the collegium minutes, Dimitrijevic talks about it, you've seen the reference in General Perisic's letter, you've heard the evidence from General Vasiljevic about what General Ojdanic told him about Pavkovic seeing Milosevic without telling Ojdanic about that. You've heard a lot of evidence from people who say that General Pavkovic was a soldier's soldier, was an outstanding officer, an excellent officer, but we say that a truly outstanding officer wouldn't do that, wouldn't go outside the chain of command, wouldn't skip over his commander to see the ultimate supreme commander. And the fact that he was willing to do so, we say you take that with other evidence in this case which shows that he was ambitious, and sometimes ambitious men are willing to take an extra step, to go a little further, and sometimes in doing so, they cross the line. We say that's what the evidence in this case supports. And certainly at this stage, there's evidence from which you can make a finding that he should be held to answer in the Defence case. Mr. Ackerman also made in connection with General Perisic the argument that: Well, Perisic's letter complaining about this isn't really all that serious because you see in July about the same time Exhibit 4D137 and -- which is Perisic's directive. But you heard a lot of discussion about that with General Vasiljevic when he was here, and Ms. Carter I believe in her re-direct examination with Mr. Crosland about that document, and I think when you read it you will see that that is not an operational order. It's a planning document, and the fact that he issued that planning document - which would seem to call for the use of the army in combatting anti-terrorism in Kosovo - doesn't undermine his position that he disagreed with how the army was being used. And it doesn't show that he's willing to use the army, he's willing to make that directive, but he wants that order from Mr. Milosevic. He wants that declaration of an extraordinary state, a state of emergency or a state of war. Mr. Ackerman said there was no ordering of crimes. Well, you wouldn't expect to see an order couched in those kind of terms. There's no need to do that, as a matter of fact, when the tactics and the units being used achieve this under the guise of a routine operation. There was a suggestion that Mr. Pavkovic had assisted the Prosecution by turning over documents, which indeed he did do. He turned over documents. I believe you have from Mr. Coo or you've seen a list of what the documents were. We would suggest that many of those are more self-serving than anything. Joint Command. The lack of reports to the Joint Command doesn't mean that it didn't exist. There are significant gaps in the record. We don't have the Pristina Corps war diary. We're missing combat reports. You heard Mr. Coo's evidence about the difficulties in actually finding Joint Command documents, and I'll talk about that again in a moment when I talk about General Lazarevic. The Joint Command documents don't match the requirements of official documents. They don't have a distribution list and there's no signature, but Pristina Corps documents and brigade documents and orders and reports do make reference to Joint Command orders in both 1998 and 1999. Certainly it was un-Orthodox, the Joint Command, but there's no sign it was fictional, quite the contrary. Joint Command orders may say "I have decided ...," but they also say "operations will be commanded by the Joint Command." And they do list roles for both the MUP and for non-Siptars. I want to turn now to General Lazarevic. Each other accused had a particular responsibility within this joint criminal enterprise. General Lazarevic provided the tactical knowledge and equipment and men to implement on the ground the objectives of the JCE. He was a commander of the Pristina Corps, the primary VJ body in Kosovo. We say Lazarevic planned, ordered, controlled, commanded, and encouraged the VJ Pristina Corps, the MUP, and subordinate forces in the pursuit of the objective of the joint criminal enterprise: Ethnic cleansing to alter the ethnic balance in Kosovo, to enable continued Serb control in the province. He, too, played an integral role in policy decisions in coordination of operations of the FRY and Serbian forces within Kosovo. Vasiljevic tells you that Lazarevic was at a Joint Command meeting in June 1999. Colonel Pesic tells you that he knows Lazarevic attended Joint Command meetings. And Joint Command orders were issued directing the VJ to support the MUP in operations against the Siptars. The first one I think we showed you was Exhibit P1967. The drafting similarities and style of these Joint Command orders to Pristina Corps orders exhibit a close connection between the Pristina Corps and the Joint Command. But think about it. Who is involved in the Joint Command from what we know? Mr. Sainovic, so you have a politician, a nonsoldier; we have General Pavkovic and General Lazarevic, so you have representative of the VJ; and you have the MUP, the police, General Lukic. But in terms of combat, who in that group knows how to write orders, combat orders? It's not Mr. Sainovic and it's not the MUP, even though they engage in combat activities and they do police anti-terrorist operations, it's not the same as controlling huge numbers of men and different components of forces over large areas of territory. So it makes sense that if there's someone in the Joint Command who's going to draft these orders, it will be somebody from the military, and that's why Joint Command orders look like VJ orders, look like Pristina Corps orders. It's only logical. Furthermore, General Lazarevic personally signed -- we have the stamped and signed amendment to the Joint Command order for joint combat operations. I think the amendment is Exhibit P1967 or 1966. I can't remember which one's the amendment and which one's the original. But you'll see that reference. So, clearly General Lazarevic is aware of it and appears to be recognising the authority of the Joint Command because he's not telling anybody to ignore the Joint Command orders, he's simply making an amendment to it.
