The orders from the Joint Command often include the Pristina Corps and assigns specific tasks within locations and areas where our alleged crimes were committed. Thus, as a member of the Joint Command, General Lazarevic had a direct impact on the operations that led to carrying out the objectives of the JCE. From this evidence, we say you can conclude that General Lazarevic attended Joint Command meetings to provide information and actively participate in the coordinated efforts of the JCE -- of the VJ and the MUP. General Lazarevic had de jure and de facto authority over the Pristina Corps. He assumed command on the 28th of December, 1998. That's in Exhibit P801. In addition to the forces that normally fell under him, the 72nd Special Forces Brigade and the 63rd Brigade were also under his command. This was part of the increased manpower that came into Kosovo and, we say, in anticipation of the spring offensive. General Lazarevic exercised effective control over the Pristina Corps by ordering and making changes or amendments to directives and orders issued by the Joint Command and the VJ General Staff. You'll see exhibit -- an exhibit is referred to in General Lazarevic's interview, which is Exhibit P950. That is order number 455-172 from the Joint Command. Lazarevic further ordered the resubordination of the MUP in accordance with orders he had received from the army command. This authority is further illustrated by his amendment, which calls for specific steps by the VJ to support the MUP. It is 1967, I recall now, Your Honours. Other examples of his authority to issue orders and command units of the Pristina Corps include Exhibit P1503 from the 27th of May, 1999, where the Pristina Corps, the 37th Motorised Brigade from the 2nd Army and the 15th Armoured Brigade were to conduct combat operations aimed against the KLA in the Prekaz area. Furthermore, an order from the command of the Pristina Corps, back at a time when Lazarevic was still the Chief of Staff, decided that the Pristina Corps and its subordinates were to follow the orders of the Joint Command. That's Exhibit P1428. That came out in -- on the 14th of August, 1998, and, as far as we can tell, remained in place throughout the indictment period. Relating to 1998, we also see General Lazarevic in Exhibit P969, the 7th of -- or the 10th of August -- 10th of July, 1998, issuing an order to his troops not to fire if international observers were present. You'll see this is an order talking about the artillery, and we say this is evidence showing that the VJ was aware of the presence of international observers in the area, the complaints that had been made about them using excessive force, and taking steps to avoid international observers see them do that kind of thing. We say this also explains in part why a witness like Shaun Byrnes say he never saw the VJ use any heavy artillery against a village; but that's contrary to other evidence you have heard in this case about what was done in the summer of 1998. General Lazarevic, as Pristina Corps Chief of Staff in 1998, was aware that crimes were being committed by units of the Pristina Corps, and upon his elevation to commander of the Pristina Corps in December of 1998 and subsequent thereto, there's no indication that he replaced any of those persons responsible. His failure to do so, we say, indicates he intended that further crimes be committed. As we've said before in connection with Generals Ojdanic and Pavkovic, the VJ had a very elaborate reporting system and a chain of -- and a clear chain of command. Lazarevic has admitted that he would receive reports about the general situation in Kosovo. Lazarevic had first-hand operation -- had first-hand knowledge of operations of the Pristina Corps in the field from his own visits to the forward command post and from monitored radio communications of units on the ground in Kosovo. He tells us that in his suspect interview at pages 4 through 8. He often accompanied General Pavkovic, the 3rd Army commander, on unit operations -- observations and command post visits. This is also in his suspect interview, Exhibit P950. In January 1999, after he had taken command of the Pristina Corps, he continued to engage some of those same units that he had reason to know had engaged in crimes in 1998. In April of 1999, Vasiljevic tells us that he was notified by the Pristina Corps chief of security, who would have worked with General Vasiljevic and with General Lazarevic, of the possible involvement of the 252nd Armoured Brigade in killings at Mali Alas. This is referred to in Exhibit P2594 at paragraphs 54 through 58, the statement of General Vasiljevic. This unit, the 252nd, was a subordinate unit of the Pristina Corps, and yet on 25 May 1999, a month or so after this information came to Vasiljevic's attention, Lazarevic issued an order for the continued destruction of the KLA and ordered the continued use of the 252nd Armoured Brigade in that operation. We say continued use of units like the 252nd indicate that it was the intention of General Lazarevic that his troops continue to pursue the actions that led to the ethnic cleansing, deportation, and forced transfer of Kosovo-Albanians. That failure to take reasonable measures to prevent and punish only encourages and provides an environment that fosters commission of future behaviour by the same and other units. Through his position as commander of the Pristina Corps and as a member of the Joint Command, he had the authority to order the use of materials and men to implement the purposes of the JCE, and he had knowledge about which units had committed crimes in 1998 and would likely commit future crimes. He was aware of these crimes through the VJ's reporting system and from being on the ground in Kosovo. We say that evidence shows he intended the continued perpetration of those kinds of crimes. General Lazarevic further shared the intent of the other members of the JCE by actively participating in the meetings of the Joint Command headed by Mr. Sainovic, and he actively planned, organised, and ordered the use of the Pristina Corps to implement the intentions and objectives of the Joint Command. We say this is evident from Exhibit P1428, an order from the command of the Pristina Corps directing the Pristina Corps and subordinate units to follow the orders of the Joint Command. There's similar information in a 25 April 1999 combat report, Exhibit P2016. In addition, General Lazarevic gave information about the current position and status of the Pristina Corps during the meetings attended with other members of the JCE, including General Lukic, General Pavkovic, and Mr. Sainovic. He intended to participate in the JCE and to share the intent of those other members. We want to address the failure to prevent or punish. We say he was in possession of information that provided him with knowledge that there was a real or reasonable risk that crimes would be committed, and he failed to take reasonable measures to prevent future crimes. He was aware of joint VJ-MUP operations in 1998 and early 1999. He knew of excessive use of force during those operations. He certainly knew of allegations of excessive force from several sources. He received information and reports from his subordinates, from his superiors, the media, and other international organisations and observers that at least put him on inquiry notice about such allegations. General Lazarevic permitted the use of VJ troops and volunteers that previously had acted unlawfully. We refer you to the statement of Fred Abrahams in Exhibit P2228. Because he permitted and facilitated the commission of these crimes through his position as commander of the Pristina Corps, we say he aided and abetted the JCE. Without the support of the Pristina Corps, the objectives could not have been achieved. They were the primary tool in this joint criminal enterprise. He willingly provided material support to the JCE, and he provided informational and strategic support to the Joint Command. He had knowledge of the widespread crimes, he knew that his willingness to allow the use of his Pristina Corps troops was a substantial contributor in achieving the goals of the JCE. He failed to take necessary and reasonable disciplinary measures, and this simply encouraged and instigated the commission of further crimes. By so doing, we say he aided and abetted the crimes charged. I want to address some of the remarks that Mr. Bakrac made and one final comment about General Lazarevic in the Joint Command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you do that, just --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- clarify for me one thing, Mr. Hannis. In relation to Messrs. Ojdanic and Pavkovic, you've also presented the alternative to a JCE, that there was 7(1) liability for ordering, planning, and as well as aiding and abetting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You seem merely to refer to aiding and abetting in this instance.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Was that deliberate?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, that was an oversight on my part. I would make the same submissions regarding General Lazarevic as JCE, ordering and planning, as I did for General Ojdanic and Pavkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, for bringing that to my attention. Mr. Bakrac pointed out that the VJ acted professionally and cited Mr. Byrnes and Colonels Crosland and Ciaglinski for that proposition, but we point you to other testimony of General Crosland about the tactics of the VJ and that he found them excessive. Exhibit P2591, the 37th Brigade post-operational analysis from April of 1999, a reference to using an elephant to kill a fly suggests that the tactics were excessive, and thus not professional. He argued that Mr. Lazarevic was not in a joint criminal enterprise, if there was one, nor was he in the Joint Command. I want to address that last thing with a reference to his interview, Exhibit P950. But we do have evidence from Pesic and -- and Vasiljevic about Lazarevic attending Joint Command meetings. We do have Exhibit P1967, his signed amendment of the Joint Command order. Also, the Joint Command orders all specify a role for the armed non-Siptar population, which links the local defence to the VJ. And we say this helps with regard to identifying the perpetrators because we say this shows that they were all - and when we say "they all," we mean VJ and subordinate units, we mean MUP and subordinate units and we mean the local defence - they were all under control of these accused. With regard to the Joint Command, General Lazarevic was interviewed after he arrived in The Hague. At that time, he was interviewed in part by an investigator and by Mr. Coo. The OTP only had one document from the Joint Command at that time, which was shown to the witness, and he was asked about it. I'm reading from page 27 of Exhibit P950, and he's asked if he knows anything about this Joint Command or this document. He said: "Just before I wanted to tell you that on several occasions. I'm not certain whether it was more than twice there have been -- there have been a document some sort -- some kind of instruction or where even -- even the heading of the order said Joint Command, and I've seen several of these papers, these documents, but without signature. Nobody signed them. For me and a group of men at the forward command post in Djakovica, there was only the Pristina Corps command, and none of my subordinates ever asked me what the Joint Command was and whether they should listen to me or to them. Personally, I believe this was probably a technical mistake in the name. I don't know whose mistake this was, and I don't know who came up with the idea to name itself, but I would like to assure -- to assure you that this mistake had nothing to do with where I was at the time with the rest of the men at the forward command post, because if I thought anything different than what I'm saying now, I -- be assured that I would react, that I would have reacted as an officer and in 1998 already the same way I did react in 2001, when something to this but much more serious was attempted to be done in the south of Serbia when a coordination body tried to take over -- take command over the army and the police and to curb terrorism." Your Honours, we say that is difficult to swallow when you see all the references to the Joint Command, the evidence about him attending the Joint Command meetings, and the fact that he authored an amendment to the Joint Command order signed and stamped by him, it's admitted into evidence, there's really no question as to authenticity. And yet, when he's here interviewed and he's shown a document, he's trying to say: Oh, I might have seen some things like that, but I didn't know anything about them and if I thought there really was something like that, I would have taken action. Your Honour, we say that is evidence from which you can infer that he was aware that Joint Command existed, and we suggest he was aware that they were engaged in a joint criminal enterprise, just as other accused in this case have tried to run away from the Joint Command and deny its existence, it's there and it's not going away. I'm not sure why it is so sensitive, unless maybe it's because Joint Command starts with the same letters as "joint criminal enterprise." They're both JCEs, and we say there is a close connection between those two, more than an alphabetical one. For all those reasons, Your Honour, we think at this stage we have shown -- the Prosecution has presented sufficient evidence for the case to go forward on all five counts as to these accused. I'm going to shut up now and sit down, and Mr. Stamp will address the other three accused and some other matters with you. Thank you.

utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, I have a question, a little digression from all the seriousness in this. And while arguing, you pointed out that -- you mentioned about the professional army's role against rogue soldiers. And I immediately was reminded of "Arms and the Man" by Bernard Shaw and that also pertains to Balkans. Is there a relevance when he calls those he met as chocolate cream soldiers, any relevance to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm not sure, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise for interrupting you and for disturbing the order, as it were, but since Mr. Hannis gave references for all his assertions, about five minutes ago he said that the Prosecution knows that Sainovic was a member of the Joint Command in 1999. Could I kindly have a reference on the basis of what they have this knowledge so that I could share this knowledge with him? That is the only thing I wish to say. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think if you wait until you've heard Mr. Stamp's submissions, you might be in a better position to know whether there is a basis for this assertion and it would be best, I think, in any event if there are matters to be cleared up for the Defence if that's done at the end of the complete Prosecution submission. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President, Your Honours, may it please you. As indicated by my learned colleague, Mr. Hannis, I'll make submissions in respect to the 98 bis applications made on behalf of Mr. Milutinovic, Mr. Sainovic, and Mr. Lukic, and I'll also make a few general comments, comments that apply to the -- all the accused in respect to Article 7(3) liability and one or two other comments on some other aspects of the evidence which we submit also applies to all the accused, including the evidence of the disposal of bodies. There has been quite a lot of evidence tendered in this case over the last few months and there is limited time so I am going to be selective in the evidence I refer to. I will try to address you within the confines of what is expected, as Mr. Hannis submitted at this stage, that at this stage we're concerned with evidence on which a reasonable trier of fact could act and not evidence that goes beyond a reasonable doubt. We are not at that stage yet, so I will be generally referring the Court to the evidence I intend to rely on, and I will try to address the submissions of my friends for the Defence directly, even though I would make general submissions about our case as a whole in respect to the accused. So if I have missed something in respect to any of the submissions, I would be grateful if the Court has any concerns if that could be raised. And I am reminded that I should go a little bit more slowly. I wish to start, Your Honours, with the submissions made by my learned friend Mr. O'Sullivan on behalf of Mr. Milutinovic, and I, as I indicated, will respond specifically to those submissions and will also make some comments on the general evidence which I believe supports the charges in respect to that accused. I think the first and major thrust of learned Defence counsel's submission is that Mr. Milutinovic, as head of state or president of Serbia had no statutory or public authority over public administration. He was mainly, primarily a symbol of national unity, and therefore had no effective authority to exercise. And the Defence submission is that these, therefore, negate the allegations of the Prosecution in paragraphs 8 and 35 and 36 of the indictment, where we submit that he had powers to do something about what was happening and failed to do so. And I submit that there's copious evidence indicating that he had the powers, as alleged in the indictment, and that in the exercise of these powers he furthered the implementation of the joint criminal enterprise, and in omitting to exercise some of his powers he also furthered the implementation of the joint criminal enterprise. Now, clearly there are formal and de facto by looking at his formal powers, and especially those that we have referred to in paragraphs 8, subsection (iii) and 35, subsection (e) and (f), and 35 -- 36(g) and (h) of the indictment, that is his participation in the JCE and the commission of the crime by failure to act as the president. And, firstly, I'd like to look at the role of the president under the constitution of Serbia and the constitution is P855 I think there are two copies because there is also P1021. And under that constitution, the president of Serbia is a very powerful individual. He stands in a very strong position. He is directly elected by the people of Serbia under Article 86, and he can only be removed from office on impeachment by a two-thirds majority of all the members of the National Assembly. That's at paragraph 88 -- or Article 88, paragraph 2 of the constitution. And even then he can only be recalled if there is a majority of the votes for his recall at the referendum Article 88, paragraph 3 of the indictment [sic], and in certain circumstances he can dissolve the National Assembly upon proposal of the government. What are his primary duties under the constitution? Because I will come later to the importance of identifying what his legal duties are -- not just moral duties, but legal duties. His primary duties can be gauged from his oath of office. In section 86 of the constitution. And that is where he swears to devote himself to the realisation of the human rights and the preservation of the peace and welfare of the citizens of Serbia. It is very brief, if I could just read it quickly, and I should say that the articles of the constitution that deal with the powers of the president are -- are not very lengthy, and I would ask Your Honours to look at those powers because they indicate what figure the president of Serbia and what powers and authority he had in the circumstances of the allegations of this case. His oath of office was: "I swear that I shall devote all my forces to the preservation of sovereignty and integrity of the territory of the Republic of Serbia to the realisation of human and civil freedoms and rights, to the observation and defence of the constitution and laws, and to preserving the peace and welfare of all citizens of the Republic of Serbia, and that I shall conscientiously and responsibly meet my duties." Preserving the peace and welfare of all citizens of Serbia. In paragraph 88, the constitution provides that the president of Serbia shall be responsible to the citizens of Serbia. So how does the constitution of Serbia enable the president to discharge this paramount of all responsibilities, the preservation of the human rights and peace of its citizens? Your Honours, the constitution at section 85 invested in him significant oversight powers, mainly, as we have alleged in paragraph 8, subsection (iii) of the indictment, to request any organ of government, the MUP for example, to state its viewpoint concerning questions falling within its jurisdiction; in other words, for them to report to him on what they were doing in the exercise of their governmental functions. It was submitted by learned counsel for the Defence for Mr. Milutinovic that that should be construed with the provisions of the Law on Government, which is P1862. But if Your Honours have a look at that, insofar as is relevant the Law on Government provides, and this is Article 19, that: "At the request of the president, the government shall take a position on certain issues within its jurisdiction and inform the president thereof within a time he determines being not less than 48 hours." So basically all the Law on Government does is regulate the time. It gives the government organs 48 hours to report to the president. So, Your Honours, the Prosecution's position is that this was not an exercise in idleness as if he was given a responsibility as president, a burden to carry without any power, any authority to achieve it. He could have intervened to protect the peace and welfare of the Kosovar Albanian citizens of Serbia, if he so wished. He, himself, recognised that, because in his statement or in his interview to the OTP, he agreed that in March 1998, in respect to the Jashari incident -- and that is an incident that is referred to in the indictment, the paragraph I can't recall just now on the pre-trial brief. Mr. Milutinovic says that when he heard about that incident, he called officials, including the minister of interior, and had them brief him about it. This was in March 1998, sometime before the JCE -- the joint criminal enterprise crystallised, as we -- we allege in the indictment. So not only did he have this significant oversight power, but he knew that he could exercise it and how to exercise it. And this, on a fair reading of his interview to us, at all times when he exercised his constitutional power to call the minister of interior to account for incidents in which Kosovar Albanians were persecuted. So before I move on, if I may just briefly address on the law in respect to this issue. The existence of the mode of liability of commission through omission under Article 7(1) of the Statute of the ICTY has been acknowledged in the jurisprudence of the Tribunal, and that is a Kvocka appeals judgement at paragraph 187. Requirements are an omission or a failure to act, an ability to act, and a duty to act. In other words, it goes beyond just a moral duty of an individual to stop oppression, but there must be a duty under some rule of law. And the authorities are the Blagojevic and Jokic trial judgement and various cases cited in that judgement, as well as from the -- the appeals division of the ICTR, the Rutaganira trial judgement at paragraph 68 and the Ntagerura, N-t-a-g-e-r-u-r-a, et al. appeals judgement at paragraphs 3, 34, 35. Now, it is sufficient, Your Honours, that the accused acted -- or may I repeat it. It is sufficient that had the accused acted, he or she would have made it more difficult for the other members of the JCE to implement. The head of liability for commission by omission has been applied to aiding and abetting in Krnojelac appeal judgement at paragraphs 37 and 43, to instigating in the Galic appeal judgement recently upheld at paragraph 168, and the duty to act should be assessed on a case-by-case basis. The source of the duty can arise in various circumstances. In this case, as I have submitted, it arose under the constitution, the primary law of the Republic of Serbia, but it also arises on the international humanitarian law that a head of state or a head of government or a president of a republic has towards its citizens. In addition to omission by commission as part of the -- or commission by omission as part of the actus reus for participation in the JCE or the other forms of commission under 7(1), Article 7(1), a Trial Chamber may infer the intent to commit an act or to commit the crimes from the omissions. The Trial Chamber in Galic at paragraph 722 held, and I quote: "The omission by the SRK" -- that is Sarajevo-Romanija Corps Command -- "indicates that the accused had the deliberate intent to allow the situation and behaviour to continue." The deliberate intent. The Trial Chamber also held at paragraph 745 that: "The inference is compelling that the failure to act for a period of 23 months by a corps commander who had substantial knowledge of crimes committed against civilians by his subordinates and is reminded on a regular basis of his duty to act upon that knowledge bespeaks a deliberate intent to inflict acts of violence on civilians." And this was upheld by the Trial Chamber -- by the Appeals Chamber. Outside the context of military superiors, this principle also applies. It's a common-sense principle, and it has been recognised also in the jurisprudence of the -- of the Tribunal. In the Simic case, the Defence argued that Simic had no authority over persons committing crimes; however, the Trial Chamber found that Simic, as the highest-ranking civilian in Bosanski-Samac municipality, had the opportunity and responsibility to protect non-Serbs from crimes. And that's paragraph 994 of the Simic trial judgement. The Appeals Chamber at paragraph 108 of its judgement re-affirmed that as president of the Crisis Staff, Simic had an obligation to try every possible measure to prevent non-Serbs from being persecuted. The Appeals Chamber further held that Simic failed to take significant steps to prevent the continued arrests and detention of non-Serbs, and from this the only reasonable conclusion that could be drawn from its aforementioned findings is that he did so with a discriminatory intent. And it re-affirmed the Trial Chamber's position that the only, only, reasonable inference to be drawn in the circumstances from those facts is that Blagoje Simic shared the intent of the participants of the joint criminal enterprise. So the duty and the implications arises under the constitution of Serbia and on the international humanitarian law in respect to a high official or a position -- or an official holding high public office to protect civilians from persecution, and from this it is submitted respectfully that a Trial Chamber could infer that Mr. Milutinovic not only encouraged and promoted, instigated the crimes as alleged by contributing to the environment of impunity, but also intended the crimes charged in the indictment and intended to participate in the joint criminal enterprise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I ask you two questions? Is the only source of the duty to which you've referred what is said in the oath of office?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The -- the oath of office of the constitution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The only source in the constitution for that duty --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- is the oath of office?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The oath of office, and the section 88 in which he is responsible to the citizens of -- of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And second question I have is, you said that commission by omission is recognised where there's a failure to act, a duty to act, but there was a third element and that was the ability --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The ability.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- the ability to act. Now, what do you say ought to have been done?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The -- I was coming to that, but the responsibility of the president under the constitution, the power he's given under the constitution, is a power to raise an alarm, really, in the corridors of government. The test, as enunciated in the cases that I cited, is whether or not by doing something, anything at all, as I indicated about the Simic case, he must try everything possible, whether by doing something it would have made it more difficult for the carrying out of a joint criminal enterprise. Here the constitution said he could call up the minister and say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- what about 250.000 Kosovar Albanians being made internally displaced people, persons? What about these villages that we are told being flattened? What about this United Nations resolution about the excessive force by the police against one sector of a society? What about the various reports that he got from the leader of the Kosovar Albanians, Mr. Rugova? Various international figures complaining about specific incidents. He --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Your Honours. So in examining the evidence, particularly in respect to the JCE, the joint criminal enterprise that had developed, and I refer to the joint criminal enterprise because the law in respect of the joint criminal enterprise is that the contribution need not be substantial once it makes it more difficult -- once by doing something, it makes it more difficult that he has contributed to the JCE. The question is whether the president could have exercised his formal or de facto power, and I want to discuss there in respect to the power -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I'm confused by your last submission. You said that by doing -- the contribution need not be substantial once it is -- once by doing something, it makes it more difficult that he has contributed to the JCE. I don't understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours. I -- the submission is that insofar as a law in respect to joint criminal enterprise is concerned, one's contribution or part or participation in a joint criminal enterprise as a member need not be substantial, as in this case the contribution by omission is sufficient as long as it makes it more difficult for other members of the joint criminal enterprise to implement or to perpetrate the crimes in the joint criminal enterprise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I thought the submission was the opposite earlier, that his obligation was to make it more difficult for members of the JCE to act, and that's what would have taken him out of the JCE.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: His obligation was to act to make it more difficult. I just expressed it in the reverse.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, okay, if that -- I'll accept that the first version was what you intended. Thank you. Are you trying to say that it's sufficient as long as it does not make it more difficult for other members, or are you confusing what's necessary for involvement in a JCE with what is necessary in the form of failure to make you a member of the JCE?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I'm not confusing the two at all. The submission is that as far as a joint criminal enterprise is concerned, one's act of participation need not be substantial --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- the participation of a -- of anybody who is a member of that JCE need not be substantial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In this situation, we are speaking about participation by omission. It is sufficient that had he done something, it would have made it more difficult for the other members of the JCE to carry out the JCE.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That was your original submission. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So, if I may, Your Honours, with your leave move on to his role in the Supreme Defence Council, because he also had powers as a member of the Supreme Defence Council. It seemed to me that the submissions of my learned friend for the Defence was that the Supreme Defence Council was merely an advisory body. The president of the republic exercised all the authority over the VJ and could, whenever he wished, accept or not advice from the SDC. The Prosecution's submission is that as a member of the Supreme Defence Council, Mr. Milutinovic had significant powers as well to affect or prevent the perpetration of these crimes, and that he either failed to exercise these powers, to impede the joint criminal enterprise, or when he did, he did so in agreement with Mr. Milosevic to further the joint criminal enterprise. Just a side note. I think it was Mr. Fila who submitted for Mr. Sainovic that the -- it was the SDC that exercised command functions over the army; whereas the position seems to be slightly different as submitted by Mr. O'Sullivan for Mr. Milutinovic. The FRY constitution, the -- and that's the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia Law on Defence, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia Law on the VJ, all demonstrate that the SDC was a body which made decisions which governed the armed forces, that is the army, and not only advised. These laws show that the SDC had the authority to make decisions in respect to military issues, including the activation, deployment, the command system in the VJ. And all the laws provide that the president of the republic shall act in accordance with these decisions. The operative word is "shall." That is, the president of the republic has no discretion to act outside of the directives of the SDC. The SDC was the highest civilian body with responsibility for national defence and employment of the VJ. Under the FRY constitution, that is P856, at Article 135 it is stated that the VJ shall be under the command of the president of the republic, that's the president of the FRY, pursuant to the decisions of the SDC. The FRY Law of Defence at paragraph 985 states in Article 40: "In accordance with the decisions of the SDC" the president of the republic commands the VJ in wartime and peacetime. And Article 8 of the same Law of Defence, P985, states that in a case of an imminent threat of war, a state of war or a state of emergency, the president of the republic shall, pursuant to decisions of the supreme council, order measures of readiness, mobilisation and use of the armed forces of Yugoslavia. Similarly, Article 41 of the Law on Defence provides that the SDC renders decisions in accordance with which the president of the republic commands the Army of Yugoslavia, that the SDC determines the strategy of armed conflicts, and rules of the use of the forces of the country's defence and the conduct of war. The SDC determines the rules on the use of the country's defence and conduct of war. The FRY law on the VJ at P984 reiterates at Article 4 that the president of the republic shall command army, war and peace in accordance with the decisions of the SDC and Article 4 states that the president in accordance with the decisions of the SDC shall decide on the deployment of the army and approve the plan for its use, determine the system of command in the army and oversee its implementation, regulate an order of readiness of the army in a state of war, issue basic regulation and other acts related to deployment of the army and perform other duties relating to command over the army in accordance with federal law. So these provisions indicate, quite clearly, that the SDC had a major element of control over the employment of the armed forces and that the president of the republic was not independent of the SDC in his management and deployment of the armed forces. Again, if we look at the minutes of the SDC. For example, the minutes of the 8th Session of the SDC, and that's P1000. It was determined that the SDC would continue to be apprised of all matters regarding the army and all remarks should be discussed and taken into account in the decision-making process of the SDC. The decision-making process, indeed, Your Honours, if you review the submissions by my learned friend, even on occasion in discussing the role of the SDC, you determine decisions in some of what it did. It was not merely advising. Not only did Mr. Milutinovic had have powers as a member of the SDC, but the minutes also show that he was an important participant in making decisions re: Some of the most important issues when we are discussing the sort of allegations we have in this case, personal issues, which commanders do you place where? Which commanders do you retire? Which commanders do you promote? He was actively engaged in making these decisions. He, himself, on occasion referred to clearly VJ-related matters. And there were discussions within the SDC of budget matters, personnel matters, and significantly the matter of replacing the highest officer of the VJ, the head of the General Staff. Mr. Milutinovic participated in the removal of Mr. Milutinovic [sic] and his replacement by General Ojdanic about whom my learned colleague Mr. Hannis has discussed. I beg your pardon, I misstated. Mr. Milutinovic participated in the removal of General Perisic and his replacement by General Ojdanic. That is in Exhibit P1576 at page 4, the minutes of that SDC meeting. You see one member of the SDC expressing reservations and Mr. Milutinovic -- as we will see of a review of many of the exhibits coming out in support of the position of Mr. Milutinovic [sic], who we allege was the leader of the joint criminal enterprise. In P1000, that is the minutes of the 8th Session, we see Mr. Milutinovic being present --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I take it your last reference is actually to Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic. Thank you very much, Your Honour, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's the reference at line 13.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: He was a participant in the elevation of Mr. Pavkovic, that's P1000, at page 10; he was present when the SDC adopted the proposal of the -- of Mr. -- of General Perisic on personnel issues, which included the promotion of Vladimir Lazarevic to major-general, and that is P1574, the minutes of the 5th Session. So it is submitted, respectfully, Your Honour, that he participated in furthering the joint criminal enterprise by the exercise of his powers within the SDC in supporting Mr. Milosevic in the placement of other members of the JCE, some of whom are charged here, to positions where they could effect and carry out the plan, the purposes, of the JCE. And if I may digress a little bit from the JCE, he exercises powers also under the law of ranks to further the JCE in the way in which under that order he could promote or appoint police personnel. By virtue of Article 6 of the law of ranks of the MUP, which is P1015, the president of Serbia was in power to appoint and promote generals and authorise officials to posts up to the rank of general is required as per the job specification. This gave the president additional influence over the police service in Serbia. He exercised his power to promote General Lukic to the rank of lieutenant-general on the 12th or at least in May 1999. My learned friend, Mr. O'Sullivan, had submitted that there's no such evidence. Your Honours, a review of his interview with the OTP at P -- that is P604, at page 186, shows that he admitted that he signed the decree promoting General Lukic on the occasion of security day, which would be the 12th or 13th of May, 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Sorry, but that document has not been placed on the file.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Because counsel was very categorical that he was not promoted, and I was also looking forward to an answer on that, but that he was promoted or was he not? And what is your position on that, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: At P00604 -- well, I believe - and I will check this and tell you in the break. I believe in the Defence pre-trial brief, Mr. Lukic did accept that he was promoted. As to whether he was promoted by Mr. Milutinovic, that is Mr. Milutinovic signing the decree, that is in the interview given to the OTP by Mr. Milosevic, that is admitted, and that is P604 and that is at page 186. And in a moment, I'll probably be able to tell you when it was admitted into evidence. On the 10th of October, 2006. We also ask ourselves the question or I submit respectful that one would ask our self a question, what does a president of a country do with the powers he would have in SDC when there are allegations of these grave crimes of persecution against an element of the population on a wide-scale basis over a long period of time. It is said that there is no evidence that the SDC, whatever his powers in the SDC was, but there is no evidence that the SDC convened after 23rd or 24th of March, 1999. However, Your Honours, if one views the rules of the SDC, and that is Exhibit P2622, that's the rules of the SDC, that is dated the 23rd of July, 1992, and P1738, that is the amended rules, the rules that were amended on the 23rd of March, 1999, those amended rules provided that the president of Yugoslavia, of the FRY, shall - shall - convene meetings at the proposal of members. So a president disturbed, and not a participant of the joint criminal enterprise, hearing these grave allegations in receipt of an ICTY indictment naming him and identifying specific crimes had the power to convene a meeting of the SDC. He did not. I think my learned friend Mr. O'Sullivan submitted that the members of the SDC, apart from the president, did not have the power to propose agenda items, as if the president of a republic would not say, Well, you know, they say that hundreds of people are -- hundreds of thousands of people have been forcibly expelled, we need to discuss that gentlemen, the president of the republic would not do so. It is the submission of the Prosecution the rules of SDC gave the president a power - and these are called common sense - a power to put on the agenda issues that he thought were of importance, and I refer to P1738, the relevant rules of the SDC, and that is paragraph 3 -- sorry, paragraph 5. Paragraph 3 provided the president shall convene the SDC, that's the president of the FRY, if any member demands it or requests it. And paragraph 5 enables a member of the SDC to put on the agenda a matter that he considers important for the SDC to determine. It is submitted that a member of the SDC who was not a party to the joint criminal enterprise could have exercised these powers in a manner that would impede the implementation of the joint criminal enterprise. Instead, the evidence is that Mr. Milutinovic joined Mr. Milosevic at every step. By failing to make use of his powers as an SD member -- SDC member as outlined above, he contributed as a participate to the joint criminal enterprise and alternatively instigated and aided and abetted the commission of the crimes. In addition, Article 4 of the relevant rules of the SDC, that's the rules that govern the period after the 23rd of March, 1999, provided that the decisions must be adopted by consensus. So he could have significantly impacted on what the army was doing on the ground in Kosovo in any SDC meeting by standing up and discharging his responsibility, sworn responsibility, as the president of Serbia. And as a member of the SDC, Mr. Milutinovic was kept informed in addition to the note that I referred to earlier in which they agreed that they must receive reports in respect to certain things, Article 2 of the rules shows that Mr. Milutinovic must have received reports from the VJ and other state organs involved in the defence of the -- the FRY. He was present when Mr. Sainovic reported to the SDC on the cooperation between the VJ and the MUP, and there was a discussion of other security-related issues and that is P1000. And if you review P1000 carefully, you will see that some of the statements that Mr. Milutinovic made, for example, when he discussed allegations of undisciplined and unconstitutional conduct of VJ soldiers and said that these allegations were inflated, demonstrates that he not only had material knowledge but he was aware of the allegations that were being made, and as an SD member -- as an SDC member dismissed them. I would about now seek to move on to another topic, so I don't know if it's a convenient time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. We shall break now and resume in an hour at quarter to 2.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.45 p.m. --- Upon resuming at 1.46 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If I could try to move along more quickly and turn to the challenge raised in respect to the existence of a Supreme Command and Mr. Milutinovic's role therein. To the extent that the existence of this body during the relevant period has been challenged, I refer the court to Exhibit 1488, an order dated the 18th of April 1999, signed by General Ojdanic as chief of staff of the Supreme Command, and Exhibit 1459, a report signed by General Pavkovic addressed to the Supreme Command staff and an order in response to it by the Supreme Command, which is P1495 and dated the same date, the 24th of May 1999, signed by General Ojdanic as commander of the Supreme Command. And General Vasiljevic also testified about the chain of command during operations; that is, and he spoke at pages 8658-8663 of the transcript of 18th of January 2007, of the reporting system that was in operation that went right up to the Supreme Command. The other reference I leave to the good judgement of the Chamber to make whatever use it will, or to give whatever weight it is, is P949, which I think was referred to by my colleague Mr. Hannis, which is the subsequent interview of Mr. Pavkovic -- General Pavkovic, I'm so sorry, in which he states that Mr. Milutinovic was a member of the Supreme Command. And Radomir Tanic in his statement, which is -- which was admitted in evidence at paragraph 109, said that when the war with NATO began, Mr. Milosevic established the Supreme Command of which Milutinovic was one of its members. I don't --

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I must object. Paragraph 109 of that statement is not in evidence pursuant to your order. You admitted paragraphs 1 to 45.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, I will ensure that it is in evidence and return to that. My information is that it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber will be able to deal with this in the light of the comment made by Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I wanted to say in respect to Mr. Tanic that notwithstanding learned counsel's submissions that Tanic is not to be believed, I'd ask Your Honour to refer back to the submissions of Mr. Hannis in respect to the standards here at this 98 bis hearing which do not involve an assessment of the credibility of the witnesses in a manner that my friend suggested the Court should -- should undertake, and that the evidence of Mr. Tanic is not so inherently incredible that it has to be discarded at this stage, as was submitted. The prosecution submits that Mr. Milutinovic attended many international meetings and conferences, many times along or in the presence of Mr. Milosevic. And in doing so, he gave legitimacy to some of these meetings and conferences by attending as the president of Serbia, and in some of them - particularly the last few days of Rambouillet and Paris, which I'll get to later - he acted in a manner which furthered the joint criminal enterprise. I think it is in respect to this position of the prosecution that learned counsel sought to suggest and argue that Mr. Milutinovic had no or a limited role in foreign affairs as a president of the Republic of Serbia. Your Honours, I refer back to Exhibit P1021, which is the constitution of the Republic of Serbia, and article 3 thereof provides that all -- that the president of Serbia shall conduct affairs in the sphere of relations between the Republic of Serbia and other states and international organisations in accordance with law. So there is some legal basis for the accused Mr. Milutinovic to undertake engagements in international affairs. However, if we look at the actual situation, the -- the fact of the situation, it is clear that Mr. Milutinovic attended many of these meetings and was present at many of these meetings as an ally and as a participant with Mr. Milosevic in the JCE. There is evidence of Mr. -- Ambassador Vollebaek in a statement at P2634, in which he said that Mr. Milutinovic's presence gave legitimacy to those meetings at -- as president of Serbia and in his testimony here, he said that Mr. Milutinovic would be present at meetings and he would normally, and I quote: "Normally, as far as I recall anyway, sit next to Mr. Milosevic and be very supportive of Mr. Milosevic and not very supportive of [inaudible]." And I'm quickly going to refer to many of these meetings without going into detail into them, but I'd ask the Court to look into the records of these meetings, look at the topics discussed, the persons present, and assess whether he was attending these meetings as a symbol of national unity, as was submitted by the defence, or whether he attended these meetings as a central figure, as a senior leader, in respect to the affairs of Kosovo and the engagements of forces of the FRY and Serbia. Mr. Tanic in his evidence stated at page 6371 of the transcript that the private chain of command of Mr. Milutinovic included Milomir Minic and Nikola Sainovic for internal affairs and Milan Milutinovic for foreign relations. Mr. Milutinovic was present in the October 1998 negotiation that led to the FRY-Serbia-VJ -- sorry that led the FRY and Serbia -- I withdraw that. This is clearly incorrect. In any case, he attended the October 1998 meetings and he led the delegations of the FRY and Serbia, the Serbian MUP, he led the MUP delegations during technical negotiations with NATO representatives and this is the evidence of Mr. Naumann. Mr. Naumann also spoke of the meeting of the 15th of October 1998 with General Clark, Mr. Solana, in which Mr. Milosevic was warned about the use of excessive force. Mr. Milutinovic was there. He spoke about the meeting of the 25th -- 24 and 25th of October 1998 with Mr. Milutinovic and Sainovic present, in which Clark issued warnings in respect of the conduct of the forces of FRY. In that meeting, Mr. Milosevic denies use of disproportionate force. This was a meeting, it should be noted and that I think was discussed earlier by my friend -- by my colleague, Mr. Hannis, in a general sense, in which Mr. Milosevic made derogatory remarks about the Kosovo Albanian people and stated that they should be killed, and it was in P2512, the transcript of Mr. Naumann from the Milosevic case. In those circumstances, Mr. Milutinovic voiced no opposition, expressed no dissent, to that sort of a -- and according to Mike Phillips, Mr. Milutinovic was present in meetings with Mr. Milosevic and Mr. Walker in October and November 1998. There is evidence of a meeting of the 19th of January 1999 of the Racak incident when Mr. Naumann, Mr. Clark -- General Clark met with Mr. Milosevic. The parties from FRY included Mr. Milosevic, Mr. Milutinovic, Mr. Sainovic, Mr. Jovanovic, Mr. Bugatic [phoen], Klaus Naumann and General Clark. And this is discussed in the Milosevic transcript which is in evidence and that the transcript of the 13th of June 2002, 6998, is the page number and also in paragraph 30 of Mr. Naumann's statement which is P2512. In none of these meetings could it be said, it is submitted, that he attended as a symbol of national unity. It is the Prosecution's submission that he attended as a senior political leader of the FRY. A participant in the discussions and the decision-making processes of the FRY in a crucial capacity. Turning to Rambouillet, criticisms have been passed about the credibility of Ambassador Petritsch by counsel for Mr. Milutinovic. Again, I will not address credibility arguments here but just to submit that there is nothing in the evidence of Ambassador Petritsch that undermines it to such a degree that it will make it inherently unbelievable or so inherently unbelievable that it must be discarded at this stage. In fact, I noted that Mr. Fila expressed a different view about the credibility of Mr. -- of Ambassador Petritsch, which is probably why we should not be debating that at this stage, because Mr. Fila said that persons such as Ambassador Petritsch could not say things that are not accurate. There you have it. Ambassador Petritsch said that Mr. Milutinovic told him that if Serbia was bombed, there would be massacres, and by that in the context it meant massacres of the Kosovar Albanians. That is evidence of intent, knowledge of the JCE. Learned counsel Mr. O'Sullivan suggested that -- quite correctly from the evidence, that Mr. -- that Ambassador Petritsch could not of himself after cross-examination recall it actually being said to him but relied upon the record, upon the diplomatic dispatch, which is Exhibit -- I'll get to the exhibit number shortly, but my friend Mr. O'Sullivan also suggested quite incorrectly, it is respectfully submitted, that Ambassador Petritsch saw the diplomatic dispatch long after the incident and just shortly before he testified here. On the contrary, Your Honours, Ambassador Petritsch first saw that diplomatic dispatch where he checked it just a few hours after the statement was made to him. In other words, that dispatch is a contemporaneous record of the events that it discusses or that it records. He was asked by presiding Judge Bonomy if it was a possibility that there was a mistake in the dispatch, and his response was, "Very, very unlikely, because you would not just write -- put something into writing about the president, the acting president or the president of a republic, part of then Yugoslavia if it were not said particularly in such a dispatch. It's an internal dispatch. Again, I must reiterate, and of course we, as diplomats, are bound to say and write the truth and nothing but the truth. That is clearly one of the main principles." And Ambassador Petritsch also told you about the system of checking the accuracy of these dispatches before they were transmitted. We see that there has been some evidence about something similar being said by Mr. Stambuk and Ambassador Petritsch could not remember whether or not he heard it from two persons or from one person. But if one reflects on the evidence in this case, it is clear that more than one person at some point in time during the development of the joint criminal enterprise expressed in moments of high tension or anxiety, expressed a knowledge that something was going to happen in the spring of 1999. So that is evidence before you, that the ambassador could not remember whether there were two statements or one statement, but he did remember or he could testify that he could rely on that record that he checked. Again, his credibility was challenged in respect to his evidence about the transparency of the process at Rambouillet, in that, firstly, it is the position of the defence that the implementation chapters were tabled just hours before the Serbian delegation had been forced to sign. It is the evidence of Ambassador Petritsch, and this is a matter to be determined at the end of the case - we're not now dealing with proof beyond reasonable doubt - that those tables were made known to the Serb delegation or the Serbian delegation from the 19th of March. And that's at transcript 10841 and 101925 -- well, and I think this is transcript 10925 as well. The other complaint about Ambassador Petritsch, which is again an issue of credibility, is as regards side letters. It is said that Ambassador Petritsch should not be -- or his evidence should not be received at this stage because the talks were not transparent, because there were side letters going around between various parties. This doesn't affect his credibility, and although I'm not addressing the credibility issue, I'll just say this. As regards the side letters, his testimony was that these are not unusual in bilateral or multilateral negotiations of this nature. What he knows is that he had nothing to do with any side deals or side letters. He had nothing to do with the Kosovar letter addressed to -- to Secretary of State Albright, and he did not participate in the event depicted in the video sequence which was shown by the defence in which there were letters being prepared and one party, the Kosovar delegation, was not allowed to see those letters. And that, as far as he was concerned, he and the representatives of the Contact Group conducted themselves fairly and transparently in respect of both parties, and they had no control over what other persons from other states might have tried to do, in terms of influencing proceedings. The significant thing about Mr. -- or Ambassador Petritsch's evidence is that whatever those implemental -- those implementation provisions were, they were open for discussion. The peace could still have been salvaged. There was no need for outright rejection of further talks. That is a gravamen, it is submitted, of his testimony. And although Mr. Milutinovic, at the beginning, was not formally a member of the Serbian delegation, when he attended, he played an important role at Rambouillet and later at Paris - particularly at Paris - where he led the negotiation on behalf of Serbia and where he led the rejection -- I beg your pardon, on behalf of the FRY and where he led the rejection of any agreement. According to Ambassador Petritsch, and also we see from the evidence of Veton Surroi and Ibrahim Rugova, deceased, he undermined and directly obstructed these negotiations and was clearly acting on the directions of Mr. Milosevic. And later on, on the 23rd of March, 1999, he addressed the Serbian Assembly and persuaded them, particularly the majority party, just his party in the assembly, to -- to reject the Paris accord. It is the Prosecution's submission that in so doing, he furthered the objective of the joint criminal enterprise because, as my colleague Mr. Hannis has described, the plan, as expressed from before, was to bring a solution to the Kosovo problem by the spring, by March, of 1999. And at the time, when these -- the peace proposals were rejected, that was the time when the forces of the FRY and Serbia was ready to go on the offensive to effect the plan. I noted that Mr. Fila, in his address, suggested that Mr. Sainovic was removed from his position because he -- or dismissed, I think was the expression, because he disagreed with the programme. That is not the evidence, Your Honour. The evidence is simply that by that time, by the time of the Paris talks, Mr. Milutinovic took over and led the rejection of the peace proposals. I'd like to do a quick review of Mr. Milutinovic's de facto powers. We have been looking at powers which are mostly supported by law. As I submitted earlier, he was a central figure in the proceedings relevant to this indictment, and by his participation at important meetings of the military and security apparatus responsible for what was going on in Kosovo and the reports that he regularly received -- that he would regularly receive from senior personnel involved in affairs of Kosovo, he could not have been a participant as a national symbol as suggested, a symbol of unity. He could not have been there as a guarantor, when you look at these meetings. He was there as a party, in the Prosecution's submission, to the planning and the ordering of the force of the FRY and Serbia, to conduct the operations which are the subject of these indictment -- of this indictment in Kosovo. Again, it is a matter for Your Honours to give this whatever weight you think it's worth, but Exhibit P605 is the interview of Mr. Sainovic, and he said that in the first half of 1998, he was sent to Pristina on several occasions and would report back and consult with Mr. Milutinovic. That's at page 9. Colonel Pesic in his statement, P2502, attended a meeting in 1998 in which Mr. Milutinovic was present with Mr. Lukic, Mr. Pavkovic. He concluded that Mr. Milutinovic was present as a guest of the Ministry of Internal Affairs, and the issues they discussed was related to the political and security situation in Kosovo. K64, in his statement at P2805, states or stated that at the MUP staff for Kosovo and Metohija meeting held on the 5th of November 1998, Mr. Milutinovic stated that the Joint Command for Kosovo would remain in the same composition as when it was set up. He -- it was clear that Mr. Milutinovic supported the existence of the Joint Command and advocated its continuing function. So Mr. Milutinovic de facto, in his capacity as president, as well directly lent support to the authority of the Joint Command and their activities and its legitimacy. Again, K64 said that Mr. Milutinovic also attended another MUP staff meeting on the 23rd of September 1998, in which in his address he told them that terrorism in Kosovo was defeated and only minor terrorist groups remained. And Mr. Sainovic, in his interview at P605 also discusses the -- well, here he discusses the conduct of Mr. Milutinovic. I will not go into that, this one. Similarly, Mr. Lukic in his interview at P948 also mentions the presence of Mr. Milutinovic at MUP meetings, the MUP for Kosovo meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we objected to this, and you have given directions to the prosecution that perhaps they shouldn't be referring to the statements of the co-accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, we haven't given them directions, Mr. O'Sullivan, we've have expressed, or at least I have expressed, a preliminary view about what the law might be on this, and we'll take account of the arguments when we decide whether any of this is admissible against your client. And you will have the opportunity, if you wish, to respond to it as you asked for earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I just leave it at that. The Tribunal -- the Chamber may give it whatever weight you think it. There was a meeting on 29nd of November 1998 of the operational interdepartment staff for the suppression of terrorism in Kosovo, and the minutes of that meeting are P2166. Present at the meeting were Slobodan Milosevic, Mr. Milutinovic, Mr. Lukic, General Pavkovic and Mr. Sainovic. This document gives significant insight into the level of detail of the -- of reporting that these persons, including Mr. Milutinovic, would receive. Indeed, General Lukic, who was present at that meeting, gave a detailed report in the compliance of the MUP with the Holbrooke-Milosevic agreement. In his interview, that is the interview of Mr. Milutinovic, P604, he said that during the NATO campaign, he had maybe two or three meetings with Mr. Milosevic and the chief of the General Staff together. Your Honours will no doubt have a look at what he says. This is at page 68 to 69 of his interview, because he seems to at first deny meeting both of them together, but that is a matter for you. He says, I should add, in his interview that these meetings, they are told the consequences of the bombing. He also said in his interview that there were also frequently half-hour meetings reviewing the general situation with Mr. Milosevic, and the general leadership held in Velesboro [phoen] Palace. It's at page 69 and 74. That the minister of defence was present at these meetings, and that he was informed at these meetings about what was happening in Kosovo, although he adds at page 70, "not in detail." At page 76, he explains that these meetings were held for historical reasons because during the war, previous war, there were circumstances where the leadership appeared to have -- and that is World War II, 1941 to 1944, appeared to have left the country at some point in time. Much of what he says in the interview about these meetings are a matter for interpretation, but what is clear is that he was meeting with Mr. Milosevic during the bombing, and he was meeting with Mr. Milosevic in the presence of the senior figures, the leaders, of the operation in Kosovo, although in the interviews, to be complete, he says that he met them for a variety of reasons. I move on very quickly to the evidence in respect to the passing of the decree, that's P993, the decree in respect to identification cards. The answer to that, which it is submitted again would probably be worthy of more consideration if we were discussing proof beyond a reasonable doubt at later stage, was that this law was repealed after the war. Well, it was repealed after circumstances had changed significantly, after it had had its effect and could have had no further effect in disabling, as it clearly did, or discouraging expelled Kosovo Albanians from returning to Kosovo. Quickly to submit, Your Honour, that it is clear on examination of these meetings that his presence and participation in the circumstances of what is happening in Kosovo, that he knew about, and that's what I would come to now is his knowledge, indicates that he is a central figure who participated in the planning and the directing at a high level, a political level, of these operations, as my colleague Mr. Hannis indicated that operations on the ground, it would be other members of the JCE who would have that role of making direct orders to the force on the ground. Clearly, Mr. Milutinovic not only had inquiry notice, inquiry notice of the various complaints he would have received from the international media, from the United Nations resolutions, but he would have specific direct notice from the ICTY indictment of the specific offences. There is also the evidence of Mr. Rugova, the deceased leader, former leader of the Kosovo Albanian people, who said in mid-April 1999 -- he complained to him about the expulsions of Kosovo Albanians from Kosovo; that is the leader, the recognised leader of the Kosovar Albanian people making a complaint, something in the nature of an official complaint to the president about the expulsion of the Albanian people. He said that Serb police and military forces, paramilitaries and other volunteer forces were driving the Albanians out. This is a report, a complaint, that has great significance and carries with it serious ramifications in the present circumstances. We have the evidence of Fred Abrahams about letters he sent to various ministers in the Serbian government, P540 to P546, letters he sent to various organs of the Serb government. He also said in his testimony that the Human Rights Watch sent reports to the various organs and specifically to the presidency of Serbia, and this is at page 76 to 78 of the transcript. I think either Mr. Hannis or myself has already referred to the reports made by Mr. Naumann and General Clark in October 1998. There is P02827, an internal memo from the Deputy Minister of Information to the office of Mr. Milutinovic, dated the 1st of October 1998, in which he describes media reports regarding criminal acts being committed by MUP personnel in Gornja Obrinja, Glogovac as propaganda and suggests possible response. Now, although it is described, these reports are described as propaganda, it shows that Mr. Milutinovic received reports analysing what the international media was saying about the use of excessive force by the police and the army, the FRY. Dusan -- Dusan Loncar, at P2521, states that there were incidents around Podujevo, Racak, Stimlje, et cetera, where he had to organise meetings. He attended these meetings with Milan Kwarter [phoen], Colonel Mijatovic, Velimir Slana. These meetings were recorded by Velimir Slana, who made five copies of these meetings and distributed them to -- to, and their addresses included Nikola Sainovic and Mr. Milutinovic. P508 is one such report, a report by Velimir Slana in which he states that DZ had brought to the attention of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs office in Pristina that FRY and Serb forces were acting in a disproportionate way. This report was sent to Slobodan Milosevic, Milan Milutinovic and Nikola Sainovic, among other persons. And P399 is a letter from the prosecutor, the then prosecutor of this Tribunal, Louise Arbour, dated the 26th of March 1999, to Mr. Milutinovic expressing her grave concerns about serious the violations of international humanitarian law in Kosovo. Mr. Adnan Merovci also in his evidence testified about personal reporting to Mr. Milutinovic about offences committed against the Kosovar Albanian people. That has a -- that's a transcript 8412. And he was also present when Mr. Rugova made the reports that I've already discussed. There are -- and I just give exhibit numbers, there are a significant amount of other documents detailing Mr. Milutinovic's receipt of notice or reports or information about what was happening, including P1481, P2828, P2842, P2843, P2844, and these documents confirm that there was a regular system where the senior political leaders would be informed about what was happening in Kosovo. So it is submitted that Mr. -- the evidence is, there is serious evidence on which this tribunal could act that Mr. Milutinovic acted with the necessary intent for all the offences charged. That he had the necessary knowledge in respect of all the offences charged. And that by his actions and his participation -- in particular his participation along with Mr. Milosevic in the various meetings I've discussed, and his omissions, he participated in the commission of the crimes. I will discuss in a general sense issues in respect to 7(3) liability for high government officials, especially where de facto responsibility is concerned and I, with the leave of the court, would do so after I have discussed the evidence with respect to Mr. Sainovic who is another high government official, and just do it in a general sense in respect to both. I had referred earlier to the Simic decision. This is a very important decision because Simic, unlike Mr. Milutinovic, did not have a constitutional role and power but he was held to have a legal power under international humanitarian law as a high government official to do anything he could, to use his political influence in any way, to stop what were massive crimes that were being committed, the crimes in Kosovo were greater, not that I minimise the crimes in Bosanski Samac. And it is important to point out, in addition to what I've said about that case, that ultimately, the Trial Chamber found that any high political leader in that position, who felt that he could not or would not do anything, for whatever reason, ought not to have occupied the position and not done anything but ought to have resigned. Ultimately, Mr. Simic's failure to resign in the circumstances of what was happening in that municipality was also an indication of his intent and his participation. Your Honours, I wish to move on to evidence in respect to Mr. Sainovic and the submissions made by my learned friend, Mr. Fila, in respect of Mr. Sainovic. I'll do it this way, with your leave. I'll proceed to deal with the specifics of his submission first and then, having regard to the time how I'm progressing, I will deal with my general submission about the evidence in respect to Mr. Sainovic. I'm not sure if I need to. It's some tribunals require that you respond to the specific submissions that are made in the no-case submission, and I intend to start by doing that, but I will, depending on the time, come back to some other matters that, about the evidence of the prosecution, that perhaps Mr. Sainovic did not mention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The second part of what you propose to do is very important. It may be that all that's said by Mr. Fila is wrong but so what? You have to point to positively to the evidence which creates a sufficiency for your case.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. On occasion I might have mentioned K64. I'm reminded that that is a witness, Ljubinko Cvetic, that the protective measures had been withdrawn just before he testified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The Prosecution submits that Nikola Sainovic, like Milan Milutinovic, is liable within Article 7(1) and Article 7(3) for the campaign to modify the ethnic balance in Kosovo. He participated in the JCE as a civilian superior, as Mr. Milosevic's facilitator and implementer in Kosovo and shared the intent of the joint criminal enterprise, to ethnically cleanse Kosovo in order to ensure continued Serbian control over the province. Further, as a civilian superior, in a position of de facto and de jure authority, Mr. Sainovic failed to exercise his power and breached his duty to prevent subordinates from committing the alleged offences, and failed to exercise whatever powers he had to prevent -- sorry, to punish subordinated -- subordinates after the fact. Looking first at the submissions by learned counsel, Mr. Fila, a number of issues were raised. Again it is my submission respectfully, with respect to Mr. Fila, that most if not all of his arguments were arguments that went to the issue of proof beyond a reasonable doubt, which is not the applicable standard here. And I will refrain from entering into a debate weighing the value of the evidence and just proceed by referring Your Honours to the relevant evidence in respect to the areas that were addressed by Mr. Fila and the areas of the Prosecution's case that the evidence supports. Mr. Sainovic's -- sorry, Mr. Fila's submissions can be summarised under eight general heads and, of course, there are other things which I'll come to later but the submissions of Mr. Fila fall under these eight heads, it is submitted: One, Mr. Sainovic -- or the evidence disclosed that Mr. Sainovic was a middleman who conveyed positions of high ranking officials. To that, I say that is part of the allegation in the indictment, but we do not allege that that was his only role. The second head is that there is no evidence that Mr. Sainovic was Mr. Milosevic's representative in Kosovo. Thirdly, and this was probably the main thrust of Mr. Sainovic's submission, is that there's no evidence that in 1999, Mr. Sainovic was head of the Joint Command, if it existed, because Mr. Sainovic also seemed to cast doubt on it or seemed to -- to suggest or argue that there is no evidence that the Joint Command existed. So he is saying that there was no evidence that in 1999, Mr. Sainovic was head of a Joint Command and certainly not after the 23rd of March. He also said that the documents referring to the Joint Command are from the VJ and refer solely to army units. If those documents, according to Mr. Fila, if those documents are authentic, he said the evidence was that the MUP of Serbia was fully under the jurisdiction of Serbia, that's head 5. Head 6, that the Prosecution had failed to prove the existence of a vertical chain of command involving Sainovic. Head 7, Sainovic could not have known about the crimes. 8, that many persons, international figures, had complimentary things or expressed approval about the conduct of Mr. Sainovic. In dealing with this, I would like to refer to the evidence of Mr. Vasiljevic in a little bit of detail because I think if I read three paragraphs from Mr. Vasiljevic's testimony, all but the last of these heads of submissions of Mr. Fila would be rebutted. Certainly, at this stage of the proceedings. Because it is submitted that the evidence of Mr. -- of General Vasiljevic is evidence on which this Tribunal can act, on which this Chamber can act, more so that in respect to much of what I'm about to read, he was never seriously challenged in cross-examination about it. In his statement, which was received in evidence, and I'll get the exhibit number shortly, he said he attended a meeting of the Joint Command of the 1st or the 2nd of June 1999. Now, this was way into the -- this is way after the 23rd or the 25th of May. It was attended by VJ and MUP personnel; the head of the Kosovo government; by the temporary Executive Council; the head of the security services for the Pristina Corps; Colonel Stojanovic; Zoran Andjelkovic, who was head of the TC; General Djordjevic of the MUP; General Stevanovic of the MUP; General Lukic of the MUP; General Pavkovic; General Lazarevic; et cetera. It was in a building with an underground area, and it was in a large room which he, as a general, former general of the VJ, with his experience assessed to be some sort of Pristina Corps headquarters, possibly the forward command post of the 3rd Army, but it was certainly a high level operational centre. Before I proceed, this is Exhibit 2594, and I am looking at paragraph 78 to 82. He said that all the persons named except Sainovic -- Mr. Sainovic and Mr. Andjelkovic were there. When Mr. Sainovic and Mr. Andjelkovic entered, everyone rose, small talk stopped and they got down to business. Mr. Sainovic sat at the head of the table.
